high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy/vice-president of the commission. − mr president, thank you very much indeed for your kind words. honourable members, i asked for this debate to be able to update this house on the situation in haiti following the terrible earthquake of 12 january. the losses are devastating and the damage is enormous. up to three million people have been affected by the tragedy, and the death toll continues to mount. this is a massive humanitarian and political disaster. our immediate focus is on working with the united nations and the haitian leadership to ease the suffering of the haitian people. our commitment to rebuilding haiti is long term. many european citizens have also lost their lives, and around 1 000 are still unaccounted for. the eu has responded quickly, not seeking headlines but with a total focus on getting help to the people in need. on advice from the united nations, we resisted the urge to travel to haiti immediately. that would only have diverted attention and scarce resources away from the relief effort. we will of course travel to haiti as soon as it is appropriate, and i have agreed with commissioner de gucht that he will travel to haiti this week to extend the eu’s condolences and underline our commitment to the people. he will also take the opportunity to review our aid efforts so far and discuss with the united nations and our people on the ground the most pressing needs for the weeks and months to come. in the mean time we continue to work flat out on all tracks: humanitarian, political and security. over the past days, i have been in constant contact with secretary of state clinton, with the united nations leadership, with eu foreign ministers and with canada, which is leading the ‘friends of haiti’ group: all this with a view to ensuring an effective and coordinated international response. i will travel to the united states this week to follow up on this and other issues with the united states administration, and with the un secretary-general and others in new york. the un has asked for urgent financial aid – usd 575 million – as well as logistical assistance to transport humanitarian aid. yesterday, the united nations secretary-general asked for police and military reinforcements of the un peacekeeping mission as well. to help mobilise and coordinate our response, i asked the spanish eu presidency to call an extraordinary foreign affairs council yesterday. for the first time since the lisbon treaty entered into effect, we are now pulling together the efforts of the commission and the council secretariat, and the member states, in a comprehensive approach, under my overall coordination. this is ground-breaking. we had a productive council meeting yesterday. everyone agreed on the need for a rapid response and close coordination with the united nations. in terms of financial assistance, the council reached the following conclusions. it welcomed the commission’s preliminary commitment for immediate humanitarian assistance of eur 30 million, in addition to eur 92 million in preliminary commitments by member states. it welcomed the commission’s preliminary commitment of eur 100 million for early non-humanitarian assistance, for instance in rehabilitation and reconstruction, and it took note of the commission’s preliminary indication that eur 200 million would be available for longer-term responses. it called for, in due course and after post-emergency needs have been fully assessed, an international conference on haiti. in total, this is a big response in a short time. assistance will be targeted, too, to the dominican republic. finding enough money is going to be less of a problem at the moment than getting it out to the people who need it. we must ensure that it is properly targeted towards sustainable political and physical reconstruction. following the un secretary-general’s request for help with transport of humanitarian aid and for additional police units, the council invited me to identify eu member state contributions and make proposals for this mobilisation. i am working on this. we convened a political and security committee meeting immediately after the council meeting to follow up. early indications of member state contributions are already now available, including possible contributions through the european gendarmerie force. work will continue in the council preparatory groups during the coming days with a view to a rapid, targeted response. the foreign affairs council will meet again next monday. we will follow up on haiti and consider further actions. this is a major test of eu foreign policy in the new world of the lisbon treaty. the people of haiti – and our own people – expect a swift, effective and coordinated response. this is what we believe we are delivering. i look forward to working with parliament on this and am pleased to be here today to give you this information and to hear your views.
member of the commission. − mr president, let me start by underlining the unprecedented nature of this disaster – in terms of humanitarian impact but also in terms of the impact on the country as a whole. haiti is one of the poorest countries in the world. it is a country in a chronically fragile situation whose existing basic functions and capacities have been very seriously disrupted. also, the international community has been hard hit. staff of the united nations and ngos and our own commission staff are still missing, and this also explains the difficulties of organising aid on the spot. people have to understand that it is not out of a lack of competence, but because the aid community has itself been hit. relief operations are not flowing as speedily as one would wish, although one sees that this is getting better by the hour. in other words, this is not only about saving human lives. we have in fact to save the country as a whole. that is why the high representative, cathy ashton, called for this extraordinary council meeting, which was a very useful tool in addressing the problem. let me just very briefly focus on four main challenges. first, we have of course to address humanitarian needs. these are enormous and concern chiefly emergency medical care for the injured, water and sanitation – because there is risk of cholera, for example – food and shelter. what is lacking most is surgery, primary health care and drugs, water treatment kits, food assistance, emergency shelter and logistics support. what is in enough supply is search-and-rescue capacity. the organisational coordinating effort’s priorities are to complete the needs assessment, to have a better picture of the detailed needs and to organise the transport logistics. that will also be addressed within the framework of the eu institutions. lastly, we have to organise the coordination of international relief efforts. that is always very difficult in these kinds of circumstances. let me stress that, only hours after the earthquake, european echo and mic teams were deployed on the spot. they have been working there ever since to contribute to needs assessment and aid coordination. we are working with teams from ocha, a united nations organisation, and are in constant contact with john holmes, the un emergency relief coordinator. the second point is to build, or rebuild, the basic state capacity. this is very important. this country has to function again, not only physically – most of the buildings have disappeared – but with a lot of high officials having gone missing and state structures having been severely disrupted. the council welcomes the fact that we will urgently send a team of eu experts with the specific task of assessing the most critical needs of the haitian state and civil administration in order to provide technical assistance. our diplomatic and cooperation staff on the ground are of course best placed to do that, but their capacity is overstretched. this is something that will become more and more important in the coming days. as the european union and the european commission, together with the council, we could play a leadership role in re-establishing state institutions physically, and also in terms of people. third is, of course, the plan to reconstruct the country, where we have to look beyond the immediate relief phase. in a few weeks many emergency teams and means deployed at the present time will have left and there is a risk – very typical of this kind of disaster – of a second-wave disaster if we do not sustain our assistance and support. we must immediately set up massive, coordinated medium- and long-term common eu response plans for the crisis. our services are working on this. this should be designed to ensure a proper division of labour among eu institutions and member states and to ensure a linked relief rehabilitation and development approach, with a sustained and seamless transition between immediate relief and post-emergency response. we have been calling all the member states to fully engage in these efforts, and to turn into actions all our commitments for coordination and aid effectiveness. this is a time when the strength of our commitments will be tested and must come out strong if we are to succeed. lastly, the financial response. as the high representative has already outlined, the european commission will make a major contribution, first of all in terms of humanitarian aid – eur 30 million, of which the largest part – eur 22 million to be exact – is completely fresh money that comes on top of the already existing humanitarian engagements we have with haiti. the early recovery assistance – which is not humanitarian assistance, and what i just said about the state institutions of course comes under this umbrella – amounting to eur 100 million, with a 50-50 balance between money redirected and fresh money, and then the longer-term reconstruction assistance, where there is now an initial amount of eur 200 million. then we will have to see where we stand. now one is hearing figures in the region of usd 10 billion. that seems a lot to me, and in any case cannot be matched by the commission budget. we will have to see with the pledging conference and with the member states how exactly we are going to eventually participate in higher sums. that is the eu-wide package that has now been prepared on top of all the contributions that are already being made and will be made by the member states. as the high representative said, i will be going to the region – haiti and also the dominican republic – tomorrow morning to have discussions with the authorities, including on the efforts to try to rebuild the state institutions. the president and major ngos are on the spot. i will also go to the dominican republic. it is important that we also see those authorities, because they are the neighbours. you can already see that the situation might eventually create some overstretching at the border, so i will also see the dominican authorities. that is all i have to say at the moment. on my return i will report back to the development committee, on the monday afternoon.

the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the revision of the cotonou agreement gives us an opportunity to learn from the crises we are facing: the economic and financial crisis, the social and food crisis, climate change and the energy challenge, the persistence of extreme poverty. the dominant "any market" economic model and our lifestyles have not only shown their limits, they have caused these unprecedented multidimensional crises. we must therefore radically rethink all our policies. the report submitted to you today, which was adopted unanimously by the members of the committee on development, seems to me to be a first step towards this necessary re-foundation. the first imperative to be respected is consistency. the european union's trade, fisheries and agriculture policies must be designed in a coherent way to ensure sustainable development, combat poverty and guarantee a decent standard of living and income for all. i regret to say that this is not the case today. by making trade an end in itself, rather than a means to its development policy, the european union is sacrificing the people of developing countries to its multinational corporations. the negotiations on economic partnership agreements are rightly controversial among acp governments, trade unions and civil society, who see them as a threat to their economies. the agricultural question is one of the most problematic and remains dramatically neglected in the cooperation between the european union and the acp countries. while rural areas and the sector account for more than 60% of the population and their jobs, their share of eu funds for acp countries is almost non-existent. that has to change. how could we eradicate poverty without making food sovereignty a priority? agriculture must be at the heart of the european union's development policies. helping developing countries, in partnership with local farmers, to secure their food sovereignty is simply essential, especially as the democratic legitimacy of their governments is now threatened by a particularly worrying new phenomenon, the acquisition of arable land by foreign investors following the increase in food prices in 2007. china, saudi arabia and qatar now own thousands of hectares in developing countries. the european union and the acp countries must take up this issue, which is likely to generate violent conflicts and hunger riots, in particular by elevating access to natural resources such as land and water to the status of a fundamental and inalienable right of the local populations. another issue that is close to my heart is that of tax havens. the consequences are far from being unnoticed in developed countries, but are far worse for the economies and political institutions of developing countries. the illicit financial flows they allow would thus represent up to ten times the amount of official development assistance. stopping this bleeding is a matter of consistency and credibility. a first step could be the signing of a binding agreement, requiring multinational companies to automatically declare their profits and taxes in each country where they operate, thus limiting the abuse and losses suffered by developing countries. finally, i would like to take this opportunity to emphasize again the democratic deficit of this revision, for which our parliaments were not consulted. the role of the acp-eu joint parliamentary assembly must be strengthened. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i hope that the negotiators will take the opportunity afforded them to make the necessary adjustments to this partnership so that it can be a success, with the people of the acp countries as the first beneficiaries.

acting president of the council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am here today to share with you my impressions of the outcome of the copenhagen summit and the challenges it poses both for the european union and for the spanish rotating presidency in the first half of 2010. the european union's environment ministers reflected on these issues last weekend and i must say that there is broad agreement on the will to make further progress, particularly on three issues: building on the outcome of the summit, with a view to making it operational as soon as possible; strengthening its elements within the united nations; working towards our global emission reduction targets. we share goals and strategy. our immediate tasks will therefore be to complete the process of formal communication of our commitment, to consolidate a framework for action comparable to that of other industrialized and emerging countries, and to make use of all the tools at our disposal, both internally and in our relations with third countries. the december summit, which was extremely complex and marked by arduous procedural discussions, ended up focusing on the so-called 'copenhagen agreement'. the document adopted has the personal involvement of a large number of heads of state and government and leaders of regional groups, representing the will of countries whose emissions account for more than 80% of those produced on a global scale. its participants include all industrialised countries, the major emerging economies and a significant number of particularly vulnerable countries. and it should help us to answer the many questions that still hang over the formal process that should lead us to legally binding solutions, within the united nations, preferably in mexico. as regards the content of the agreement, i think it is important to stress the express support for a temperature increase of no more than 2 degrees celsius. this is probably one of the strongest and most responsive elements: the commitment of all industrialized countries to set a reduction target applicable to their entire economy. the emerging economies, on the other hand, will take concrete and verifiable actions to substantially reduce their emissions growth: the solidarity financing, aimed at supporting immediate and medium-term actions in the fight against climate change, the elements aimed at guiding new governance schemes, as well as mechanisms that support technological development and the reduction of emissions due to deforestation. the copenhagen summit has highlighted the new international scenario in which we are moving, a scenario in which improvements are necessary if we are to provide answers to global problems. the rules for decision-making need to change to adapt effectively to new times and needs. we have the necessary tools to act: a legislative package already in place at community level, a commitment at the highest level to deepening emission reductions, international solidarity and technological innovation and cooperation, the appropriate internal institutional structure, which we must use wisely, making the most of all its complementarities. we will need to combine the environment council's leadership in negotiating and designing climate change policies with enhanced external action capabilities. we must also link the environmental task with our authorities' reflections on economic and innovation policy, and strengthen the coherence of our climate objectives with our model of development and well-being. all this without losing sight of the need to consolidate, within and beyond our borders, the role of public opinion and of legislators committed to the need to invest in a better future and to protect the collective interest. let us bring our european experience to bear. first, we must have an adequate response by 31 january. the copenhagen agreement, by including all those who must reduce emissions, is making progress in the area of comparability of efforts, comparability demanded by the european union, but we still do not know the extent of the commitments of the others. if that is not enough, we must continue to work to deepen collective reduction. we will also have to create the conditions for the rapid implementation of the elements of the agreement. it is essential that the european union and its member states take the lead in keeping their word. we must therefore make the transfer of resources, which was committed for the period 2010-12, as soon as possible. we want to develop a financial architecture capable of underpinning our solidarity commitments with third countries in the green climate action fund in copenhagen and, alongside that, drive forward the progress on accounting rules, the response to reducing emissions from deforestation and on technological cooperation. in addition, we must have our own policies to meet our national and community emission reduction targets, promote innovation and the intelligent use of energy, integrate adaptation measures into sectoral policies and ensure the consistency of our external action. in all this we want to work closely with the commission and parliament, with the aim of building the world's most advanced region in the fight against climate change and the least carbon intensive, the best prepared to face the challenges posed by climate change and the most effective in making it a powerful driver of innovation and competitiveness. the policy of combating climate change is one of the main hallmarks of the european model. we have been pioneers in integrating this principle into our proposals for fairer and more sustainable development, not only economically but also socially and environmentally, knowing that in this way we are strengthening international security. this has allowed major players such as china and the united states of america to sit at the same negotiating table and identify and share key elements of cooperation. the european union, as a strong supporter of the role of the united nations in solving global issues, will also have to work in other contexts, bilateral or multilateral, formal or informal, helping to better understand the opportunities, listening to our partners, collaborating in the consolidation of sectoral responses, consistent with the needs of climate change. the adoption of the lisbon treaty and the entry into operation of the new institutions must be fully exploited, systematically incorporating the main messages of the fight against climate change into our relations with third countries. we have a lot of work ahead of us. the spanish government, aware of the scale of the challenge, wishes to express here its commitment to making the most of the elements which will enable an ambitious and binding agreement to be reached in mexico. we cannot waste the political momentum created in copenhagen, nor allow our aspirations, nor those of the international community, to deteriorate. our credibility is at stake. we must hold firmly to our position. the new and increased powers of the european parliament, which bring it even closer to the citizens, will enable us to cooperate more intensively and more fruitfully. i would like to conclude by congratulating them on this and reminding them that we need their work and support more than ever in these crucial six months ahead.
member of the commission. − mr president, let me thank you on behalf of the commission for the chance to discuss the outcome of the copenhagen conference on climate change and the follow-up to the copenhagen accord. my colleague, stavros dimas, has asked me to apologise on his behalf for not being able to be here himself because he is ill, which is particularly regrettable as this would probably have been his last plenary appearance. i volunteered to substitute for stavros in this very important debate. i want to express our appreciation for the active and supportive role the european parliament played before the conference and at the conference itself. the contacts with your delegation throughout the conference proved most useful. in particular, you have played a crucial role in order to enhance our outreach with key players in other countries and other regions. i believe we share the view that the result of copenhagen falls badly short of our goal of an ambitious and legally binding agreement, which would be necessary to limit climate change to below 2°c. this is extremely disappointing for all of us who have fought for years and years for concrete policy decisions to reverse climate change. the reasons for the failure were many and i will come back to them in a moment. still, one may also conclude that the accord is better than no outcome at all, which would have been the worst-case scenario. on the one hand – to find something positive – the copenhagen accord at least recognises the need to limit climate change to below 2°c. it also invites the developed countries to list economy-wide emission targets by 31 january 2010 and calls for the developing countries to list mitigation actions by the same date. furthermore, the accord sets the basis for a rather substantial financial package of usd 30 billion for the coming three years and recognises the need for usd 100 billion annually by 2020. on the other hand, the accord has serious weaknesses. it contains no reference to mid-term or long-term mitigation targets. the reduction pledges announced so far are not sufficient to stay within the target of 2°c. there is unfortunately, in my view, little cause for optimism that we will see improved offers by 31 january – rather the opposite. last, but certainly not least, the accord is not legally binding and, perhaps even more worrying, it does not provide for the conclusion of a legally binding agreement this year, which was one of our key goals. looking ahead, the next step will be to ensure that this accord will at least become operational and will pave the way for a new climate treaty, which must be agreed on urgently in the course of this year. as a very first step, it will be crucial to ensure that all key parties now endorse the accord and notify their targets or actions by 31 january. adequate financing also needs to be provided. in this respect, we need to explore ways of setting up a copenhagen green climate fund. we must also strengthen alliances with countries and regions who share our vision of a successful outcome in the international climate negotiations. to conclude, we have huge challenges before us to ensure unity at the european level, to engage strategically with key external partners and to maintain our full commitment to multilateral climate action, but there are many lessons to be learned from cop15. one striking lesson certainly is that we must learn to speak with one voice. in copenhagen, china, india, the united states and other major powers each spoke with one voice, while europe spoke with many different voices. the same goes for global economic governance and international security. we are indeed at a crossroads today. either we take determined and united action for europe’s ecological, economic and political revival, or we risk economic stagnation and political irrelevance. let us take copenhagen as an alarming warning of that scenario. we must do better than that and we can do. only by standing united can we succeed, and i look forward to working with you to achieve this objective.

mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, thanks to the work of mr domenici, the report on which we are finally voting this week is a very good document. i very much hope that it will be adopted by our plenary on wednesday. many of the advances it contains in financial transparency, tax policy and the fight against tax havens, the far-reaching consequences of which are rightly highlighted here, are simply unprecedented. firstly, it is to be welcomed that the text acknowledges the considerable limitations of the fight against tax havens as it has been carried out up to now. the oecd tax conventions and lists of non-cooperative jurisdictions, to use the official language, are not satisfactory and are part of the problem they are supposed to combat. the proposals in this report to go beyond this approach, to adopt a new definition of tax havens and to put in place new tools to combat this, including sanctions, are therefore of paramount importance. this is clearly the case with the proposal to introduce an automatic exchange of tax information, both within the european union and at international level. this is also the case with the country-by-country accounting required by the report, which will make it possible to measure the real activities of companies in the countries where they are established and to verify that they are paying the taxes they are legally owed. these are two essential claims which have long been defended by many experts. we can only be pleased that the european parliament is taking them up and is thus becoming one of the institutions most committed to this fight. the problem of tax havens is not just a technical one. it refers to fundamental choices. do we want to give developing countries the means to benefit from their own resources instead of having them confiscated? do we want to ensure that all our companies and citizens contribute to the financing of our collective life to the extent of their means? by voting for mr domenici's report, we will give a positive answer to both of these questions. an answer, i think, that we can only be proud of. and i want to personally thank commissioner kovács for the seminar we co-organised in brussels on 9 december to put this on the agenda. thank you and good luck.

acting president of the council. - madam president, we are facing a situation in the euro area that is unprecedented because it is the first global financial crisis since the euro has been introduced, and what is happening in this euro area and in the european union as a whole is that, without having caused the crisis, without being the place where the crisis originated - we know it was in the united states - we have suffered from it as much as the country where it originated. it is clear that the situation of government deficits has been brought about as a result of the above and the positive action of governments to avoid, among other things, the collapse of the financial system. and these deficits inevitably reduce the room for manoeuvre of governments in their budgetary policies. the debate is on the economic situation, the monetary situation and the social situation. as regards the economic situation, the euro area as a whole has already emerged from recession and the risk of deflation has also been avoided, although the inequalities in growth rates are obvious and, moreover, growth is still not entirely sustained. it must be sustained and consolidated - and this is an essential objective of economic policy in the euro area as a whole - but this recessionary situation has been abandoned. the euro area as a whole is no longer in recession. and, in any case, it is true that job creation is lagging behind. there will still be a tough unemployment situation in the euro area as a whole this year, but growth is moving in the right direction. in fact, this is one of the elements that will be discussed at thursday's informal european council meeting: the importance of growth in order to return to sustained growth, to maintain the european social model and to start creating jobs again, in this case quality jobs. as regards the monetary system, despite some tensions on the stock markets, the european union and its institutions have acted correctly. the european central bank has done and is doing its job well, graduating exit strategies. it is therefore reasonable that the incentives should not be abandoned during 2010. the european central bank is in fact phasing out these incentives, gradually phasing out some of the measures it has already adopted, for example in relation to the liquidity advantages granted to banks, and this is thanks to the fact that credit markets have been normalising. on the other hand, it must also be said that the eurogroup and ecofin have managed the crisis well and, moreover, have created an architecture for the supervision of the financial system which is going to be debated in this house and which we hope will be one of the central elements of the political debate during this six-month spanish presidency. as regards the social situation, the consequences of high unemployment throughout the eurozone are obviously being suffered, which, although also unequal, is undoubtedly reflected in the main demand of europeans at the moment: the demand for jobs; a return to growth that allows employment and employment, in this case, of quality, not a volatile or precarious employment that may have existed in some of the euro countries. among other things, it should also be noted that it is clearly the high level of employment that has triggered the so-called 'automatic stabilisers', which has given rise to unemployment benefits and subsidies, and which in turn has influenced the deficit in the member states as a result of our political and social system, which protects those who are most vulnerable, such as those who lose their jobs. in future, 'it will also be another of the topics to be discussed at the informal european council meeting on thursday', we will have to pursue an employability policy, what we call 'europe 2020', as a model for growth and quality job creation. in conclusion, madam president, i think that what has emerged in this case is that coordination and strengthening of the eurozone have been absolutely vital, that the eurozone remains an important place of monetary and economic protection, that it must be strengthened and that enlargement of the eurozone will be possible when there are countries in a position to meet the requirements, but that enlargement is also positive. and secondly - and with that, i conclude - it is essential to move in the direction of integration and economic convergence in the european union. there are still inequalities in economic positions in the union. we must move from monetary union to a genuine economic union, as the treaties say. the treaties spoke of economic and monetary union - that is how it is defined - but monetary union came before economic union. the coordination of economic, employment and social policies is in the treaties: it is an obligation and it is one of the principles, one of the lines or ideas, which the spanish presidency has put forward. coordinated public policies have been effective when they have been really coordinated: when the european economic recovery plan was made, when fiscal policies have been made around maintaining the credibility of the stability and growth pact, which has been vital, or when financial policies have been made coordinated, for example, bank guarantees or the increase in deposit guarantee funds. it is, in short, that what economists call 'economics of scale' should also be done at the political level, because at the political level coordination means good results. this is the council's view of this difficult situation, but it is one from which we are emerging and from which we must emerge in a much firmer, much more solid way. this will certainly be one of the main objectives of the informal european council meeting in brussels on thursday.
vice-president of the commission. − madam president, the commission is concerned about the substantial economic and fiscal challenges that greece faces. the difficult situation in greece is a matter of common concern for the euro area and for the eu as a whole, as large and persistent domestic external imbalances threaten the macrofinancial stability of the country with a serious risk of spillovers into other parts of the euro area. the greek authorities and the greek people are aware of the challenge in front of them. on 15 january the government presented an ambitious stability programme intended to tackle these issues. the programme envisages a deficit reduction from an estimated 12.7% in 2009 to below 3% in 2012, starting with an adjustment of four points of gdp this year. this programme displays an appropriate degree of ambition given the sheer size of the consolidation needed and is a front-loaded programme. in more detail, the greek authorities have announced a package of concrete measures for 2010. some of these measures have already been submitted to the greek parliament and are to be implemented shortly. plans for the later years of the programme are less detailed at this stage. last week, on 3 february, the commission adopted an integrated approach and surveillance mechanism which combines our assessment of the stability programme, a recommendation on the excessive-deficit procedure to bring the budget deficit below 3% in 2012, as the government established in the programme, and another recommendation using article 121(4) of the eu treaty for the first time to ensure that greece’s economic policies are consistent with our broad economic policy guidelines and with the proper functioning of our economic and monetary union. we have also started an infringement procedure to ensure that greece addresses the problems that have prevented the reporting of reliable budgetary statistics until now and the commission announced its immediate initiative on audit powers for eurostat. as regards the stability programme, the commission fully supports greece in its efforts to redress a difficult economic and fiscal situation. the measures and policy intentions outlined in this programme are an important step in the right direction. the successful large government bond issue on 25 january seem to indicate that market participants share this view, albeit at a high interest premium, and increases in the spreads thereafter also show that they remain cautious. however, there are risks to the programme targets and the medium-term fiscal adjustment. the macroeconomic scenario outlined in the programme is rather optimistic and there is some uncertainty about the underlying revenue projections, especially the estimated impact of efforts to tackle tax evasion during an economic downturn. given recent market developments, interest and expenditure projections also seem to be on the low side. as far as the recommendation on the excessive-deficit procedure is concerned, our recommendations as regard measures to be taken this year rely fully on the measures announced by the greek authorities in their stability programme. they include measures to be implemented in the first quarter of this year, such as wage-bill cuts, reduction in public employment, progress with health-care and pension reforms, tax and excise duties increases and tax administration reform. some of the fiscal consolidation measures have already been submitted to the greek parliament and should be implemented shortly. the greek authorities are invited by the commission in our proposal to the council to present by mid-march a detailed implementation report announcing adopted measures and the calendar of the announced measures. an evaluation of the risks should also be carried out so that, in case risks materialise, compensatory measures should be put in place as necessary. in this context, the commission welcomes the announcement on 2 february of further measures, notably a nominal public-sector wage freeze and an increase in excise duties on fuels to safeguard the budgetary target for this year, as well as the greek authorities’ readiness to adopt and swiftly implement additional measures if needed. as regards the later years of the programme, we call for further adjustments of a permanent nature, continued tax administration reforms and an improvement in the budgetary framework. obviously, greece is also requested to further pursue efforts to improve the collection and processing of general government aid. given that plans are less detailed, we propose setting up a tight reporting system in which the greek authorities will report on a quarterly basis on measures implemented, results achieved and measures to be implemented. this tight reporting system will ensure that the plans will materialise as planned. we also adopted the recommendation to put an end to the inconsistency with the broad guidelines of the economic policies and the risks of jeopardising the proper functioning of economic and monetary union, given the continuous loss of competitiveness of the greek economy, and the widening of external imbalances as well as by the large spread in financial markets vis-à-vis benchmark bonds. moreover, co-movements in spreads in other countries are also evidence of clear risks of spillovers to other member states. in this context, greece is expected to adopt a comprehensive structural reform programme aimed at increasing the effectiveness of the public administration, stepping up pension and health-care reform, improving labour-market functioning and the effectiveness of the wage bargaining system, enhancing product market functioning and the business environment and maintaining banking and financial sector stability. what are the next steps in this very detailed process of surveillance? our recommendations will be discussed by the eurogroup and ecofin next week, and then a first report should come in mid-march elaborating on the calendar for implementation to safeguard the 2010 targets. then, on a quarterly basis, starting in may, greece should report on the way in which they are responding to the council decision and recommendation. each report will be subject to a commission assessment. it is clear that, if there are signs that risks are materialising, additional measures would need to be implemented. therefore, it is crucial that the greek government stands ready to adopt additional measures if necessary, as they have already indicated. in conclusion, we are living in an unprecedented situation but we are facing it. greece has adopted an ambitious programme to correct its deficit and to reform its public administration and its economy. it deserves support in this difficult task, and the commission supports greece. the integrated surveillance mechanism, together with the willingness of the authorities to tackle the problems, is the guardian of a successful implementation of fiscal consolidation measures and structural reforms that will put greece back on a sustainable path. timely and rigorous implementation of the budgetary measures and of structural reforms – and both fiscal measures and structural reforms are contained in the programme adopted in greece by the greek authorities – together with the tight monitoring of the situation is the key to finding an adequate solution to the present tensions in our markets.

this means that with a stability and growth pact closely centred on public finance criteria, which are quite necessary but insufficient, spain has until recently controlled its public debt and its public deficits, but at the same time allowed its private debt to explode. there was an explosion of private debt, a speculative bubble in the housing market, a recession much bigger than elsewhere and, as a result, the need to inject massive amounts of public money. this is proof that if we take a narrow view of the stability and growth pact and the governance of the euro area, focusing only on public debt, we are missing a broader view that would allow us to anticipate the next crisis and prevent it. i would therefore like to know what proposals have been put forward by both the spanish presidency and the commission to reaffirm the stability and growth pact and, above all, to integrate it into a more comprehensive framework. secondly, you say - and you are right - that there is a need for better control of public finances, that there is a need to return to more stable levels of debt. is this only, in your opinion, due to the reduction of public spending or is it also due to the ability to raise certain taxes? mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i think that the proposal by the committee on the environment, public health and food safety to include bluefin tuna in annex i to cites is too radical. i therefore condition it on three requirements which, in my view, allow a fair compromise. the first concerns the independent scientific opinion to be published in october 2010 and endorsed by the cites meeting in september 2011. i think that scientific advice is indispensable. we must be sure that the existence of the species is really in danger before we make a radical decision on the fishing and trade of bluefin tuna. secondly, it is essential to have the guarantee of the amendment of regulation (ec) no 865/2006 concerning cites, which will result in a general derogation for domestic trade in bluefin tuna. this amendment will achieve what we all want: the sustainability of our coastal artisanal fisheries, particularly in the mediterranean. thirdly, i believe that, once we decide on this listing in annex i, financial support from the european union for the seafarers and shipowners affected by the decisions is essential. finally, if this decision is approved under the conditions i have just set out, it will have to be accompanied by a significant increase in controls to combat illegal fishing. it is on these terms and only on these terms that i can accept the inclusion of bluefin tuna in cites appendix i. without these assurances, a schedule ii listing is still the least bad, if not the best, option.

in writing. all forms of slavery, whether 'modern' or not, are absolutely reprehensible. the resolution thus has the merit of seeking to defend the victims of the violence of dehumanized appetites for profit and the social and psychological misery they create. it is nevertheless regrettable that it is limited to treating victims of criminal networks in the underground economy. for human trafficking also has its legal counterpart which is no less abject. neoliberalism, with its profit frenzy, its constant competition of workers, its relocations, also exerts both symbolic and physical violence on citizens. it forces them to migrate against their will and plunges them into such distress that suicides in the workplace are on the rise. to subject citizens in this way, to reduce them to the state of adjustment variables of an inefficient and unhealthy system, tools in the service of the interests of the financial elites, without regard for and at the risk of their lives, what is this but the equivalent of the property on beings that is slavery? if we are to fight underground crime, we must also fight institutionalised crime and make the european union a union for the emancipation of citizens.
in writing. by voting on this resolution, i expressed my disappointment with the agreement finally reached in copenhagen at the end of 2009, an agreement which i consider to be insufficient, lacking in ambition and containing no quantified commitments. i also regret that the amendment tabled by my group to introduce a 0.01% tax on financial transactions, which would finance the climate effort of the poorest and most directly affected countries, amounting to eur 20 billion per year, could not be adopted. finally, to have a say in such international negotiations, the eu will have to learn to speak with one voice, so as not to miss any more opportunities to play a key role in global climate change. this includes setting ambitious targets to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by more than 20% by 2020.
in writing. the resolution includes significant progress by the right-wing groups that signed it: citing the work of the ipcc, which refers to climate change, calling for greater participation of civil society in the work of the mexico city conference, calling on the eu to push its greenhouse gas emission reduction targets beyond the 20% proposed for 2020. but they are not enough, and the praise for the carbon market makes them unrealistic. the aid proposed for the countries of the south, to which we owe a climate debt, is insufficient. similarly, the proposed target of a 30% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2020 is far from the 40% recommended by the ipcc. moreover, no reference is made to the initiative of the world conference of peoples on climate change by bolivian president evo morales ayma. yet, to date, it is the only country in the world that has proposed that people recognize the rights of ecosystems and establish a climate justice court.
in writing. i abstained on the european parliament's resolution on the copenhagen conference because it does not live up to the failure of that conference, even though the european parliament clearly condemned the european union's shortcomings on that occasion. it is true that positive measures have been adopted, such as those calling on the commission to revise its ambitions for greenhouse gas emissions and to provide sufficient funding for the fight against these gases. other amendments are unacceptable because they leave it to the market to regulate by means of pollution permits, clean development mechanisms, etc. the european union is also called upon to enter into negotiations with the united states to create a transatlantic market for polluting rights. finally, i regret the rejection of the proposal for a green tobin tax, the proceeds of which would have helped developing countries in the fight against climate change. there can be no lasting, serious and coherent solution to climate change in the logic of the system that created it. the european union must step forward and set an example, regardless of the attitude of other states. she can do it if she can afford it.
in writing. for you, good tax governance is not about fighting fraud, being able to pay taxes or using public funds properly. it is the systematic tracking of the taxpayer, mainly european, the automatic exchange of information on his bank accounts, in the absence of any infringement. and i am not talking about the big companies or the very rich individuals, who will always have the means to get through the net, but the average european. your talk about tax havens is hypocritical: no mention of lichtenstein or the caribbean, but no mention of the biggest european tax haven, the city, or those in the united states. and silence on what makes these havens possible: the tax hells that most european countries have become, sinking under debt and deficits. because public spending has exploded to support the social consequences of your economic policies and the exorbitant costs of mass immigration. because the states can no longer finance their debt except on the markets and on their terms, which means that today 15 to 20% of the budgetary expenditure of a state like france is used only to pay the interest. we will not be used as a moral alibi for such a policy.
in writing. while it is necessary to combat tax fraud, it must not make us forget that fraud alone would never have led to the economic crisis we are experiencing today. this crisis is a structural crisis of capitalism and has its source in the very logic of this system which the european elites blindly advocate. i am voting for this text because i condemn the pursuit of personal profit at the expense of the general interest. such a logic is as much present in tax evasion as in european neoliberalism, which neoliberalism is much more responsible than fraud for the failure of the millennium development goals, which are feared. vat, which is also supported in this text, is one of the aberrations of this system. it is the most unfair tax in the world, because it subjects all citizens to the same tax rate despite the huge income gaps that are the hallmark of neoliberalism. it is a pity that the text does not tackle the substantive problem and does not seek to finally put the fair distribution of wealth produced for the general interest on the agenda of european policies.
in writing. i welcome the adoption of this report on equality between men and women in the eu. this report stresses the urgency of a community initiative to combat violence against women effectively. the adoption of this resolution also incorporates two aspects which i consider to be fundamental. firstly, the recommendation of paternity leave at european level. for equality in employment, there must be equality in society and in family life. this resolution places the european commission in charge of legislation in this area. but the real big win in this vote is the reaffirmation of the right to abortion. no european text had reaffirmed this right since 2002, due to the reluctance of a part of the european right. women must have control over their sexual and reproductive rights. it is true that there is still a long way to go in terms of effective access to information, contraception and abortion, but the tarabella report must be a key reference point for the advancement of european law in this area.
in writing. yes, women face specific difficulties. but as is so often the case in this house, the best feelings lead to distorted analysis and delusional propositions. the report thus portrays a caricature of a european society marked by daily and systematic hostility towards women: stimulus policies are sexist because they help sectors with a male-dominated workforce, budgetary austerity policies also because they affect feminized public sectors... on the other hand, there is absolute silence on the consequences of a massive presence in europe of immigrant populations whose culture and practices confine women to a lower status, light years away from our values and conceptions. we are also silent about the negative consequences of your 'everyone is equal' speech: women are gradually losing the specific and legitimate social rights they have obtained in recognition of their role as mothers. finally, silence on the question of parental pay, the only way to give women a real choice between working life and family life, or a reconciliation of the two. finally, when i see the hysteria which is driving many of our colleagues to impose mass and compulsory abortion everywhere, elevated to the rank of an essential value of a europe on the way to collective suicide, i regret that their mothers did not have abortions.
in writing. while i strongly oppose all the eu's negative measures and there are many , when things go in the right direction, i support them. the report makes strong demands (particularly to the european commission) for the fight against inequalities in treatment of women, the introduction of paternity leave, the creation of a year against violence against women and the right to easy access to contraception and abortion. it also stresses that women should have free access to abortion consultations. that is why i voted in favour of the report. but the best is yet to come. i can only regret the refusal of a majority of this parliament to support the creation of a european charter of women's rights, a european observatory on gender violence and an international day for equal pay. the european parliament has also failed to address the root causes of these inequalities, which lie in the economic system of the single market law that europe is organizing every day.
in writing. women are the first victims of the economic and social crisis that the neoliberal policies of the european union have generated. the crisis has also led to an increase in precarious employment and part-time work. our societies remain totally imbued with patriarchy. they are now marked by a strong return of stigmatisation on the basis of religion and women are still the first victims of these developments. it is therefore gratifying to see the european parliament putting such a crucial issue as equality between women and men on the agenda. it is a pity, however, that the text does not address the inherently unequal nature of neoliberalism. it is responsible for much of the suffering of women and sees in the widening of gender inequalities an additional means of prosperity.
in writing. the european parliament calls for a total ban on the international marketing of bluefin tuna. i am not voting for this measure, as i am elected from the sète basin. there is no consensus on this ban, neither among scientists nor among environmental associations. if such a radical ban were nevertheless to be decided in march at the international conference in doha, i would ask the european commission not to prevent the financial compensation that the states might be obliged to pay to fishermen. in recent years, fishermen have made considerable efforts to comply with increasingly restrictive quotas and to modernise their fleets. it would be indecent to force them to change their occupation tomorrow without giving them significant financial support.
in writing. i voted in favour of this resolution. one of its objectives is the conservation of bluefin tuna, which is an essential element of the balance of marine biodiversity. the ban on international trade in bluefin tuna will help us to preserve our bluefin tuna stocks, which are threatened by overfishing. europe will have to make sure that measures are taken by third countries, because how are we going to explain to our fishermen in europe that japanese, libyan or tunisian trawlers are plundering our bluefin tuna stocks legally? we must also be concerned about negotiating the organization of an exclusive economic zone which will allow small-scale fishing to continue because it does not threaten the resource.
in writing. i voted in favour of the ban on the marketing of bluefin tuna and, as a corollary, compensation for the tuna sector, provided for by an amendment which i had co-signed and which was able to be adopted in part. for example, bluefin tuna should be included in annex 1 of the convention on international trade in endangered species of wild fauna and flora (cites), subject to a general derogation for internal trade, allowing the continuation of small-scale coastal fishing, and to strengthened controls against illegal fishing. we must not only be concerned about this endangered species, whose stocks have fallen by 60% in the last 10 years, but also provide substantial aid to the fishermen and ship owners who will be affected by this measure.
in writing. bluefin tuna is threatened with extinction due to the lack of control over the overexploitation of this resource. a ban on its marketing now seems inevitable. it's meant to protect this species. conscious of the problem, many fishermen, particularly in france, have been working for years to bring their boats up to standards and to respect the fishing quotas necessary for the survival of bluefin tuna. these fishermen, already hard hit by the crisis, will be the first victims of such a measure made necessary by illegal fishing and hidden industrial sectors. the effort made by these fishermen cannot be borne by them alone. we cannot ask them to sacrifice themselves for the sake of the planet while the powers that be in copenhagen have shown that they are not doing enough. the un principle of shared responsibility for environmental problems must therefore be applied and the effort of fishermen must be compensated by a contribution from the european union. moreover, the creation by france of a genuine exclusive economic zone in the mediterranean would make it possible to protect the resource while maintaining a small-scale fishery that respects ecological balances.
in writing. scientific reports on the current bluefin tuna biomass are alarming: uncontrolled fishing on an industrial scale has seriously depleted stocks. this industrial and international fishing threatens the traditional coastal fisheries in the mediterranean. in order to avoid an ecological catastrophe, coupled with an economic crisis for the fishing sector, it is urgent to introduce a policy of international prohibition of industrial tuna fishing. my demand is to reconcile two major issues: the effective protection of bluefin tuna to enable it to survive and be marketed in the future and the support of european coastal fishermen whose economic activity is partly based on this trade. that is why i support the inclusion of bluefin tuna in annex i of cites in order to prohibit its exploitation and to avoid the extinction of bluefin tuna, but under the following conditions: the continuation of scientific expertise to know the exact state of the biomass of this species, the economic and social support of european fisheries operators and, above all, a derogation for the internal trade in bluefin tuna for artisanal purposes, in order to avoid the death of artisanal coastal fishing, which is a traditional activity in the mediterranean.

in writing. cooperation with the united states in the fight against terrorism is important, but not at any price. the agreement with the united states on the transfer of financial data is a bit like opening and reading the personal mail of all european citizens or monitoring all their e-mail exchanges on the pretext that terrorists may send letters or e-mails to each other. the agreement in question does not guarantee the respect of personal data, let alone the use that may be made of it. the risk of interfering with the privacy of millions of innocent citizens or with the perfectly legal financial transactions of european companies, simply on the orders of an administration, is not acceptable. i am reminded of the echelon case, a wiretapping system purportedly for military and security purposes which has turned out to be a formidable potential system of commercial and political espionage directed against allies. we can accept an exchange, that is to say a reciprocal transfer, of targeted data at the request of a judicial authority in a specific context. we want to help swift to break the technical deadlock which only allows it to transfer information in bulk. but we cannot accept this agreement.

in writing. nearly 10 years after 9/11, the terrorist threat is still present and airplanes are one of the terrorists' preferred instruments for striking our countries. we must find a way to protect our citizens and prevent them from becoming victims of terrorist acts. body scanners can be one way to increase security at airports and on board aircraft. but before we make a decision, we must ensure that these machines do not infringe individual freedoms and do not harm the health of passengers or airport staff. i look forward with great interest to the study which the european commission will present on this subject in march. by addressing all the different aspects of their use, this report should enable a european-level certification of scanners that ensures the protection of civil liberties and health while improving safety. in order to ensure that all citizens are afforded the same protection, i hope that, following the presentation of this study by the european commission, we will encourage the member states to reach agreement on this subject.
the s&d group. madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, europe is currently experiencing an unprecedented crisis which, beyond the economic and financial crisis, is first and foremost a crisis of the system. before i even begin to discuss the effects of the economic crisis on world trade, which is the subject of our debate, i would like to make one point clear: trade is not a victim of the crisis, it is also one of its constituent elements. we are in fact living in a period of great global imbalances, fuelled on the one hand by excessive trade deficits in some countries at the cost of growing internal indebtedness, and on the other by trade surpluses driven by exports from some countries, especially emerging countries, with domestic consumption not growing at the same pace. in addition, the policy of trade liberalization pursued so far has only exacerbated these imbalances, weakening in particular the poorest countries of the world. the latter, encouraged to specialise in export monocultures, thus found themselves unprepared for the extreme fluctuations in the prices of raw materials, the volatility of which was accentuated by international speculation. it is a strange world to set the eradication of poverty and hunger as the first objective of the millennium development goal, while at the same time speculating on the rise in the price of wheat. but today, the very same people who advocated liberalization and deregulation at all costs in the 1990s are also in a difficult situation. the ever-increasing loss of jobs, the stagnant or sometimes negative growth, the growing social crisis are all factors which make it impossible to allow jobs to disappear in the name of this cult. how can we explain to workers who lose their jobs in a crisis that the key is to maintain a deregulated business, even at the price of sudden and sometimes tragic relocations? the crisis we are experiencing is therefore a systemic crisis, which must be met by a new development model. in its current global europe strategy, the commission's vision is mainly focused on market access and liberalisation in all sectors. i believe, commissioner, that we must redefine this strategy, which has gone astray and sometimes leads to failure. we cannot boost the exports of our industries by forcing even more developing countries to open up. this would only worsen the situation in these countries, which already account for 70% of the 59 million people who lost their jobs worldwide in 2009. on the contrary, it is essential to think of a new strategy which strikes the right balance between openness, protection and support. i would like to return to these notions. these developments cannot be ignored, which are causing the united states to use its trade defence instruments more intensively or china to challenge european anti-dumping measures at the wto. in fact, when we are dealing with unfair practices, it is obvious that protection is necessary, but its principle must be assumed and defended internationally by rejecting, once and for all, the sometimes misleading accusations of protectionism. the need to support trade policies is also becoming more urgent every day, and this requires, in particular, a genuine coherence of the policies pursued by the union. policy coherence is not a debate of intellectuals, but an absolute necessity if we wish to redefine a new model of development.

in writing. faced with the slowdown in economic activity and the worsening employment situation, especially among young people, the european parliament and the commission are setting up a new microfinance facility called progress. the modem parliamentarians' action focused in particular on opening up the scheme to micro-enterprises in the social economy in order to enable these structures to develop social support services for vulnerable people wishing to set up or develop their own micro-enterprises. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environmentally friendly use of energy. in the end, a balanced compromise was reached between the commission, the parliamentary groups and the council, which provides for mixed funding (€60 million from the progress programme budgets, €40 million from new european budget lines). the entry into force of this new arrangement is a step forward which demonstrates the union's willingness to take concrete action to address the legitimate social concerns of its citizens and demonstrates the value of involving the european parliament more closely in europe's decision-making process. the modem meps welcome this.

in writing. i welcome the outcome of this vote because the safeguards for the protection of citizens' privacy were unsatisfactory in the council's proposal. the defence of civil liberties is a fundamental issue, and the fight against terrorism must be conducted with respect for them. in voting for parliament's resolution, i wanted to reaffirm that the interim agreement should be in line with the criteria of the lisbon treaty, and in particular the charter of fundamental rights. i also ask that data be collected only for the purpose of fighting terrorism and that european citizens be able to have "the same judicial redress procedures as those that apply to data held within the territory of the european union, in particular that of payment of compensation in the event of unlawful processing of personal data". i welcome this vote, by which the european parliament shows that it is fully assuming the new responsibilities conferred on it by the lisbon treaty and that it is able to resist pressure from european states, but also from the united states. this is a telling sign of the new political balance that is taking place within the european union.

in writing. i voted in favour of the conclusion of the swift agreement because i believe that this data exchange is useful. our respective intelligence services have reported on a number of specific cases where this has proved useful. the terrorist threat is present, there's no denying it, and the attempted bombing in detroit last month is a confirmation of that. so we have to be responsible. it's about mutual aid. this agreement should not be interpreted as a unilateral commitment by the eu. the union will give access to its information, but in return the us authorities will analyse this data, which cannot be done at present in europe in the absence of a european counter-terrorist financing programme equivalent to the us tftp. this agreement ensures our security and not just the security of the american territory. finally, it is a genuine international agreement, unlike the unilateral commitments that existed before. the guarantees will be binding, the application of the agreement will be assessed, and if the eu considers that these guarantees are not respected, the agreement clearly states that the parties can denounce it.

for the greens/efa group as early as 2006, the un was stating that the most vulnerable and poorest people were the first victims of climate change. women are the majority in both categories. in sub-saharan africa, for example, although women are already discriminated against in access to and control over land, the scarcity of arable land caused by droughts further reduces their livelihoods. a recent report predicts that by 2050, one billion people will have fled from a hostile environment. the precarious situation of these climate migrants, forced to take refuge in makeshift camps, raises the threat level against women. however, it must be noted that in the last 15 years, not a single piece of legislation adopted at european level in the environmental field has included a gender dimension. i therefore ask on behalf of the green group that the european union and its member states integrate the gender perspective into all environmental impact assessments, laws and policies.
we are debating equality between men and women today, 15 years after the fourth beijing conference, and at the same time as we are celebrating the european year for combating poverty and social exclusion. i would like to draw a link between the two, since it is true that women are still the first victims of poverty. in france, for example, they represent 80% of parttime work, with precarious and low-paid jobs. it is also women who, at 80%, earn less than the minimum wage, and who end up with pensions that are close to the minimum subsistence income. in addition, the average pay gap between women and men remains very high. equality between women and men therefore remains partly theoretical, and women, who also continue to face a large part of the family burden, sometimes have to work part-time, with multiple employers, and ultimately earn less than men. it is therefore essential that we have public policies that specifically target these inequalities, both in the labour market and at the domestic level, and social security systems that actively respond to women's needs. without such measures, beijing's objectives may well remain mere speeches with overly utopian aims.

for the gue/ngl group mr president, when mr simpson said in this house last november: 'although the community rail system is very safe and progress has been made in recent years thanks to market liberalisation', i almost choked. however, he added: "recent fatal accidents have raised safety concerns". since the buizingen accident, its terrible toll in human lives and the great physical and psychological suffering it has caused have been a powerful reminder that it is high time to open the debate on railway safety in earnest. let us immediately reject the idea that every accident is, by nature, unpredictable. the first factor of insecurity on the european rail networks as a whole is a direct consequence of the separation between rail infrastructure management and rolling stock management. this separation - and it must be emphasized here - was imposed against the most basic common sense by the commission in order to open up railways to competition. it's highly accident-prone. because of this separation, in the name of the highest profitability, the maintenance of the european rail network is sacrificed. you can try to save time by emphasising, as the only perspective for solving problems, the use of the best techniques of the moment. in the end, we need a different rail policy in europe. if every year there are fewer railway workers, less maintenance, less investment, less training, we will inevitably have to talk about accidents again and pay sad tributes. the real railway safety requires the union to turn the page from competition to cooperation. in conclusion, ladies and gentlemen, after this debate, no one can ignore his responsibilities. as for me, i refuse to be an accomplice to evil. no change ... the president shall withdraw the floor.
