member of the commission. − mr president, i am happy to contribute to this important debate on the innovative financing instruments and answer this oral question. regarding the options for the introduction of a general financial transaction tax, the commission intends, as announced in its eu 2020 strategy, to contribute to the debate on innovative financing at global level. it is currently working on defining and assessing different approaches, one of these being a general financial transaction tax (ftt). the ‘financial crisis responsibility fee’ proposed in the us and the ‘stability fee’ on certain assets of banks, as introduced in sweden, are other ones. as far as the ftt is concerned, it is clear that the options today differ from the initial discussions on the tobin tax, as it would cover a broader base of financial products. concerning the advantages and drawbacks of the introduction of the general ftt, the commission believes that, in assessing the different instruments, it is important to avoid the accumulation of initiatives that could be detrimental to the financial sector, and to ensure that the new initiatives do not result in the relocation of transactions to other regions, which would have a negative impact on europe’s competitiveness. regarding the possibility of implementing a general ftt in the eu if our main partners do not introduce such a tax, i would like to remind you that the imf is also, in parallel to the work of the commission, examining options, including a global financial transactions levy. this demonstrates that the subject is of a global nature and the commission believes that the best way to tackle this issue is to find global and coordinated solutions. this is our first and preferred option. concerning the use of tax as a complementary regulatory tool in the context of financial market reforms, i can confirm that the commission is considering complementarities between the tax and regulatory instruments and will pay attention to the cumulative impact of these two types of instruments on the ability of the financial sector to support economic recovery. regarding the possibility of making the financial system long-term oriented with the introduction of a general ftt, the commission is not aware of clear data or studies on the relationship between such a tax and the maturity structure of financial intermediation. concerning the allocation of revenues generated by a ftt, as the analysis on innovative financing is still ongoing, i think coming to any conclusions about revenue sharing and allocation would be premature. let me, nevertheless, emphasise that the potential revenues of a general ftt would be very asymmetric, probably located in only a few countries that have the largest financial centres. this asymmetry points to the need for global solutions, including about the sharing and allocation of revenue. finally, the timing of the different initiatives. as a first step, the commission’s services are currently examining the issue of innovative financing instruments overall. the commission will also take into account the conclusions of our main international partners in order to identify the options with the most potential. it is on this basis that, in a second step, concrete proposals with a detailed impact assessment might be launched, in line with the commission’s standard approach on better regulation.
on behalf of the ppe group. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the financial crisis we are experiencing has forced the public authorities to intervene financially with public money. in these circumstances, it is tempting to consider the introduction of a financial transaction tax. the proceeds from this tax would be used, for example, to finance the recovery and sustainable development of the economy and, initially, could be used to offset the cost of the crisis to the real economy and taxpayers. this tax would be in addition to the regulations regulating the financial sector, the elimination of tax havens or the regulations currently being drawn up on derivatives. at this stage, it is necessary to first assess the effects of taxing financial transactions. the main purpose of the oral question is to encourage the commission to examine in practical terms the various points listed in the motion for a resolution in order to give an opinion on the feasibility and appropriateness of such a tax. what you have just said, commissioner, is in line with our wishes. however, it should be stressed - as you have done - that in this approach realism and pragmatism are required. such taxation must not have a detrimental effect on the european economy or on the competitiveness of the european financial industry. more generally, it is important to highlight the consequences of implementing this taxation in the european union alone if, as some advocate, no agreement is possible at international level. and we do not think that such a purely european solution is possible.
for the greens/efa group mr president, commissioner, we are in a public finance crisis and we know that part of the solution may lie in cutting some spending but that a big part of the solution also lies in the ability of the states to raise more funds. so the question we have to ask ourselves is what kind of taxes can be increased, what kind of taxes should be increased and what will be the consequences of these tax increases. our analysis as a green group is that it is difficult to raise taxes significantly for small businesses, which are the ones that create the majority of jobs. it is difficult to raise the taxes paid by households, except perhaps by the richest, because in most cases these tax rates are already high enough, especially in europe. so the question is, what taxes are we raising? if we do not increase the tax on smes, if we do not increase the tax on households, if we do not increase vat, we must necessarily open the field. our analysis is that the financial transaction tax is ultimately the least painful tax for the european economy. it is the tax with the least negative consequences for the european economy in global competition. in addition, over the last ten years or so, the cost of financial transactions has fallen dramatically, as a result of a number of technical advances - if one can call them that - and european regulations. in fact, these decreases in transaction costs were fully absorbed by the financial industry and banks. it would not be totally illegitimate if part of the profit from the reduction of these transaction costs went to the public authorities which saved these same banks, through a financial transaction tax. it is a very ideological debate, in this parliament and elsewhere, but it is something that is quite technical. transaction costs existed before. they've been reduced. today, it is proposed to increase them again so that it is the public authorities who benefit from this technical progress and not just private actors. the question is, of course, whether the european union can take this step forward on its own. it is obvious to everyone that it would be better if it were done in an international framework. the question that arises if the united states, to put it very clearly, does not follow us is this: does this close any prospects for the european union or not? i would like to thank the rapporteur for his excellent report, which has been very helpful in this respect. at that point, yes, of course, there will be workarounds, the situation will not be perfect. but does that mean that the european union should necessarily be placed on the lowest common denominator, should make the least possible regulations in all respects and align itself with the least ambitious actor? we do not think that this will strengthen the european union's leadership in the world. it is also quite conceivable that the european union would be setting up this transaction on its own. simply because the capital flows that concern us, at some point, come from the european union, go elsewhere eventually, and return to the european union. as these flows leave and return, we have the possibility to demand traceability and to know whether or not they have paid this financial transaction tax. if they paid for it, no problem. if they haven't paid it, then we can charge an entry tax or an exit tax. we've done this for years with a common external tariff, it was in the real economy. financial globalisation requires us to do this now in the financial sphere of the economy and it is quite possible technically. what is needed is political will.

member of the commission. − mr president, i understand members’ concerns about the acta negotiations. let me first recall that we are negotiating this agreement in order to improve the protection of ‘made in europe’ innovation in all areas where intellectual property rights can be breached. if we want to remain a competitive economy, we will have to rely on innovation, creativity and brand exclusivity. that is one of our main competitive advantages on the world market. so we need the tools to ensure that this competitive advantage is adequately protected in our main export markets. we have tried to raise this issue for several years in multilateral organisations like the wto or the world intellectual property organisation. those attempts have been systematically blocked by other countries. so, despite our preference for a truly global solution, we have had no other choice but to engage with a coalition of the willing. the final agreement will only be binding on those countries that have signed, although we would of course be happy if more countries, and especially emerging economies, could subsequently join. as i said during my hearing, those international negotiations are confidential. that is not unusual. negotiations are about seeking an agreed outcome and require a minimum confidentiality in order for each party to feel comfortable to make concessions and/or to try out options before finally settling on an agreement. on the other hand, i agree that parliament needs to be adequately informed about the evolution of the negotiations. we are doing our utmost in two areas: to inform parliament, and to convince our negotiating partners to agree to more transparency. firstly, as regards information to parliament, we have provided you with the negotiating guidelines, full reports on the negotiating rounds and, in general, all the relevant documents originating from dg trade that have been shared with the member states through the trade policy committee. we have done this in accordance with the framework agreement. also, acta has been discussed several times in the committee on international trade in the last three years. let me add to this that the commission organised two stakeholder conferences on acta in june 2008 and april 2009, which were open to all citizens, industry, ngos and the media. another public conference will be organised on 22 march in brussels. i understand that you may feel that this is not sufficient for you to have a clear picture on where we stand in these negotiations. i have instructed my services to provided dedicated briefings with interested meps on all aspects of the negotiations. they will be at your disposal for discussion before and after each further negotiating round. secondly, i realise that the best way for you to know what is going on in these negotiations would be to read the draft negotiating text. this would give you a very clear picture of where exactly we are in those negotiations. as you probably know, there is an agreement amongst acta parties that the negotiating text can only be made public if all parties agree. the commission is in favour of releasing the negotiating documents as soon as possible. however, a few acta negotiating parties remain opposed to early release. i strongly disagree with their approach but i cannot unilaterally breach a confidentiality commitment. my credibility as a negotiator is at stake. nevertheless, i will see to it that, at the next negotiating round in april, the commission vigorously pushes its negotiating partners to agree to releasing the text, and i will raise parliament’s concerns bilaterally with acta parties, like the us, whom i am scheduled to meet before then. it is in the interests of all that everyone has a clear idea of what exactly these negotiations are about and even more importantly, also of what they are not about. finally, as regards your concerns on the substance, i would like to recall the main principles that are driving the commission in the negotiation of this agreement. first, the objective is to address large-scale infringements of intellectual property rights which have a significant commercial impact. it will not lead to the limitation of civil liberties or harassment of consumers. secondly, acta is only about enforcement of intellectual property rights. it will not include provisions modifying substantive intellectual property law such as the creation of new rights, the scope of protection or duration. however, it should set minimum rules on how innovators can enforce their rights in courts, at the borders or over the internet. for example, a european fashion designer, when confronted with counterfeiting of his creations outside europe, can ensure that his rights are adequately safeguarded abroad. thirdly, acta must and will remain in line with the acquis communautaire, including the current level of harmonisation of ipr enforcement, the e-commerce directive, the telecoms regulatory framework and, last but not least, the applicable eu legislation on data protection and piracy. there will be no harmonisation or changes to eu legislation through the back door. in this sense acta will have no impact on european citizens, since it will not create new obligations for the eu and no need for implementing legislation. however, it will provide our innovators increased protection in overseas markets. i am aware of the concerns expressed by some of you about the introduction of a compulsory ‘three strike’ rule or graduated response to fight copyright infringements and internet piracy. let me be very clear on this so there is no room for ambiguity. the three strike rule or graduated response systems are not compulsory in europe. different eu countries have different approaches and we want to keep that flexibility while fully respecting fundamental rights, freedoms and civil liberties. the eu does not support, and will not accept, acta creating an obligation to disconnect people from the internet because of illegal downloads. similarly, we will make sure that acta does not hamper access to generic medicines. i know there has been some controversy on the impact of eu customs legislation on trade in generic medicines. as i have already told you at my hearing, that problem will be addressed in the upcoming revision of our customs legislation. finally, you also asked about an impact assessment on acta. in fact, considering that the commission will not go beyond the acquis communautaire, we took as our basis the studies made for the 2004 directive on the enforcement of intellectual property rights and for the 2005 proposal for a directive on criminal enforcement of ipr (which was not adopted). we also considered the conclusions of the 2008 oecd study on the economic impact of counterfeiting and piracy. that study values the economy of physical internationally traded counterfeits at usd 250 billion, which is to say more than the individual gdp of 150 countries. it also contains an exhaustive analysis of the piracy of digital contents. in short, i hear your concerns and will defend them to the best of my ability. your confidence and support will help me carry this important task forward.

the rapporteur. - mr president, madam high representative, the report on the implementation of the european security strategy which we are presenting today is an annual document of parliament which takes stock of the progress of european security and defence policy and makes proposals to improve the effectiveness and visibility of this policy. this year's report is in a very special context which should make it a force for good. this particular context is marked by the conjunction of three major cycles. the first concerns the ten years of the european security and defence policy, which we celebrated at the end of 2009. the past decade has shown that europe can conduct civil and military operations in more than 23 theatres of crisis. this fundamental achievement can be further enhanced. it shows that there is a demand for europe and the union's institutional and operational political capacity to meet these challenges. the second important stage is, of course, and president albertini has just mentioned it, the implementation of the treaty of lisbon. the change in security and defence goes far beyond a strictly semantic adjustment. the esdp is becoming the common security and defence policy, the csdp, and it must acquire a new dimension. the treaty has enriched the range of instruments and fields of action for security and defence policy, in particular with the inclusion of the clauses on assistance, solidarity, permanent structured cooperation, but above all with the creation of the european external action service and the creation of your post as high representative, vice-president of the commission. finally, the third major event which marks the context in which this report was drawn up is that nato, which for 21 of the 27 members of the union remains the essential reference for the collective security of the european continent, is currently conducting the review of its strategic concept and that this reflection by nato must also lead us, the union, to define better the conditions of this partnership, which remains fundamental. in this context, the aim of the report is not so much to establish a doctrine as to provide you with a road map which is bound to evolve, for all the new institutions which are coming into being and which must learn to work together. the aim is to make the union more credible, more effective and more visible in the field of security and defence. in this respect, greater responsibility for these sensitive areas by the european parliament is essential to give full legitimacy to a policy whose primary objective is to ensure the security of european citizens. the report emphasizes the following points: firstly, it is important to remember that the european security strategy and the common security and defence policy are primarily intended to serve the european citizens, to guarantee and improve their security. this political ambition is not superfluous, it is not a flirtation. it corresponds to a need for our continent to work for its own security but also to contribute to the stability of the world around us, to deal with the crises and threats that are developing in our environment. beyond the traditional armed conflicts that persist in our immediate environment, europe must be able to state its interests and defend them against new threats, particularly piracy and cybercrime. we also felt it was important to stress the unparalleled added value of the union in crisis management, thanks to the variety of responses it provides and the balance it strikes in each of its operations between the civilian and military dimensions. i also reject the criticisms of the militarization of the union's security and defence policy which some people may make in this connection. i am a firm believer in the complementarity of the civil and military instruments at the disposal of the union, and the recent crisis in haiti, which you visited - and i believe you have seen this good cooperation - is a testament to the necessary intertwining of civil and military means to deal with natural disasters and major crises. we have been particularly keen to review all these operations, to highlight what we consider to be their strengths, but also, sometimes, their shortcomings - we must admit them in order to improve things. we also wanted to highlight several strategic regions for the security of the union and to urge the council and the commission to accelerate the implementation of comprehensive strategies, in particular for the horn of africa and the afghanistan/pakistan area. in the field of capabilities - both civilian and military - which is a crucial issue for the credibility of our policy, the challenge is to improve the union's responsiveness. we must be able to mobilise the material and human resources available to the states more quickly and more effectively. but we must also be able, through a high-performing security and defence industry which brings together invaluable technological know-how and which also represents hundreds of thousands of jobs in europe, to provide ourselves with equipment programmes corresponding the rapporteur. - mr president, madam high representative, ladies and gentlemen, thank you for all the speeches which, once again, have enriched the debate, enriched this report. i would like to reassure those who have expressed doubts, sometimes suspicions, that this report could open the door to more competition, more competition, particularly with nato, or even isolation. that is not the case at all, i do not believe it at all, and it is not in the treaty, quite the contrary. you can believe a french mep who has campaigned vigorously for his country's return to the integrated structures of nato. when we talk about strategic autonomy, what is the idea that we are developing, the policy that has been developed for the last ten years? in writing. i voted against the lehne report because the removal of accounting requirements for these micro-entities will not reduce the real costs of business and will create a high degree of legal uncertainty. such an exemption would jeopardise the trust necessary for the relations of very small enterprises (ves) with third parties (customers, suppliers, banks). it is necessary to maintain secure information for obtaining credits. without an accounting framework, bankers and other interested parties, who will always need information, may find a reason to reduce their credit. this will be detrimental to the ldcs.
in writing. the proposal before us is to allow member states to exempt certain undertakings (micro-entities) from the obligation to draw up and publish their annual accounts. i am of course a strong supporter of reducing the administrative burden on businesses, especially smes and smes. but the commission's proposal is seriously lacking in its purpose: firstly, it is not clear that the proposed system would actually reduce the administrative burden on these companies (the statistical information currently collected will have to be collected by other means), and secondly, this text, which leaves it to each member state to decide whether or not to make use of the exemption, risks fragmenting the internal market (in the highly probable case that some member states will make use of the exemption and others will not). this proposal should have been withdrawn and the question of simplifying the administrative burden for these small enterprises (company law, simplification of financial reporting requirements, accounting, auditing, etc.) should have been addressed in the context of the overall revision of the fourth and seventh company law directives, which is due to be published shortly. i therefore voted against mr lehne's report on the annual accounts of certain types of company (micro-entities).
in writing. i voted in favour of the report by mr lehne on the annual accounts of micro-entities because, although i believe the european commission's impact assessment is incomplete and insufficient, i wanted to make it clear that i am in favour of simplifying the accounting requirements for very small enterprises. it is not economically and socially consistent for a very small enterprise to be subject to the same administrative constraints as much larger enterprises. very small enterprises represent more than 85% of european enterprises, and thus the bulk of our economy, which is in urgent need of vitality. i therefore think that a harmonised reduction in their obligations is a good thing, but it must be ensured that they do not hinder their access to credit. the thinking should therefore be conducted in a global manner, taking into account the whole economic environment surrounding very small enterprises, their relations with banks, with management centres at the french level and of course with their customers. let us not always think in terms of obligations but let us trust our contractors, our artisans, who need us to lighten their administrative burdens.
in writing. i voted against this proposal because it risks, in the long run, turning against smes, depriving them of the conditions of transparency and trust necessary for their management and the dynamism of their activity by reducing their access to credit. i think that we cannot demand more transparency from the banks, blaming them for the lack of transparency in the financial markets which led to the current crisis, and at the same time want to remove the transparency tools which are indispensable for the economic actors themselves and for the economic regulatory policies which we want to pursue at european level. however, simplification of accounting requirements for smes, and in particular for the smallest of them, remains an imperative necessity. the european commission must urgently review the fourth and seventh accounting directives, as it is the only body capable of providing a comprehensive, fair and consistent response.
in writing. i voted against the proposal for a directive on the annual accounts of certain types of companies adopted on wednesday 10 march 2010. while i am in favour of a significant reduction in the regulatory burden on smes, i nevertheless believe that accounting requirements are also essential management tools for their external partners (banks, customers, suppliers, etc.). the proposal ultimately risks depriving smes of the conditions of transparency and trust necessary for their management and the dynamism of their activity by reducing their access to credit. it is paradoxical to ask banks to be more transparent, blaming them for the opacity of financial markets which led to the current crisis, and at the same time to want to remove the transparency tools which are indispensable for economic actors themselves and for the economic regulatory policies which i support at european level.
in writing. the 2020 strategy is intended to replace the lisbon strategy. it is also likely to prolong the shortcomings, to be followed by the same lack of results and to cause the same disappointments. it is neither a genuine recovery strategy nor a new direction for the union's economic, social, budgetary and fiscal policies. the accumulation of good intentions is matched only by the absence of new instruments to implement them. europe needs a different ambition, and citizens expect more convincing answers. since the start of the crisis, there have been 7 million more unemployed. the banks are speculating again, no regulations are passed on hedge funds and citizens are being asked to tighten their belts, public services are being cut and social protection is being cut. the greek crisis is a sign of the lack of solidarity. that is why europe must debate a different vision of its future, based on genuine economic coordination, solidarity, a strategy for green growth, an energy community, a cohesion budget, own resources, investment in education and research, fiscal and social harmonization, the fight against tax havens, the taxation of international financial transactions.
in writing. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, after the crushing failure of the lisbon strategy, which was supposed to make europe the most competitive knowledge-based economy in the world by 2010, here is the eu 2020 strategy, which is the exact continuation of it. flexibility of the labour market, i.e. precariousness for workers, increased competition at european and world level, liberal reform of national social protection systems, full respect for the stupid stability pact... all the ingredients are there to make this strategy a strategy of national and social disintegration, like the lisbon strategy before it. the only new things are those inspired by your new whims: to make european economic governance compulsory and binding, whereas the europe of brussels has shown itself to be completely ineffective in the face of the world crisis; the european union is not only a political force, but also a political force. we shall vote against this text.
in writing. i voted against this resolution because the objective of full employment is not sufficiently emphasised. secondly, our priorities should be more focused on the fight against poverty and sustainable growth. the european parliament also misses the opportunity to stress the need to combat all forms of precarious work, through a directive on parttime work, the introduction of a framework of social rights guaranteed regardless of the type of employment contract and measures to combat abuses in subcontracting, even unpaid traineeships. finally, this resolution ignores the need for the harmonization of the tax base, which is essential for the creation of a european social model. this is a great missed opportunity for the european parliament in building a social and sustainable europe.
in writing. i voted in favour of the resolution calling for the implementation of the recommendations of the goldstone report as it is essential to get the israeli and palestinian authorities to conduct impartial and transparent investigations into the tragedy in gaza in 2008-2009, not with relentlessness but with determination. the member states, for their part, must take a stronger stand and commit themselves to supporting these demands with their israeli-palestinian partners. international humanitarian law must be respected by all parties to the conflict and the eu's objective must be to ensure that these principles are respected.
in writing. reducing the israeli-palestinian conflict to a comparison of the number of deaths on either side of a warring party can only distort the view of this war which has now gone on for too long. we all agree that the solution to this conflict is difficult to find, because the causes of the conflict are complex and deep-seated. manichaeism cannot be the rule in this part of the world. the only mandate of the mission led by judge goldstone was to identify violations of international law. and although the conclusions of this report are not all unjustified, to vote against these resolutions which approved the conduct and conclusions of a text which, i believe, was conducted in a biased manner, but above all with incomplete objectives, seemed to me the most honest intellectual solution. yes, we must expose and stop the abuses by either of the warring parties in this region, but we must be very careful about the procedure we use if we want justice in this region to lead to a lasting peace.
in writing. the goldstone report highlighted the need for independent investigations to be carried out swiftly in order to establish the facts, the responsibility of the parties and the consequences of possible violations of international and humanitarian law in the gaza conflict. these investigations must be carried out in good faith by the palestinian and israeli public authorities and i hope that they will thereby be able to encourage the resumption of negotiations, and therefore fully endorse the principle of this. i would also like to point out that the conflict in gaza has destroyed many eu-funded projects aimed at alleviating the humanitarian crisis affecting the population, which is suffering from shortages of basic necessities and lack of access to basic public services. the people there need hope and to continue to believe in a speedy solution to the israeli-palestinian problem. only in these circumstances will the conditions be met for a just and lasting peace between a viable, secure and peaceful palestinian state and a neighbouring israeli state.
in writing. the french delegation modem reiterated its wish to have an impact study and concrete proposals from the european commission on the creation of taxes on financial transactions. the resolution adopted by a very large majority (536 votes in favour, 80 against and 33 abstentions) on wednesday was supported by the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection. we ask the commission to draw up a proposal to define a common european position to be presented to the g20 in june. it would also be appropriate to assess the extent to which such a tax could contribute to stabilising financial markets. the questions to be answered by the commission concern the use of this tax to support developing countries' adaptation to climate change and the financing of development cooperation, but also what levers the commission could use to persuade its partners to also implement this tax in order to avoid capital migration. but first and foremost, a thorough impact assessment is needed to ensure that this tax does not reduce the union's competitiveness, sustainable investment, innovation and growth, or have a negative impact on smes and individual investors.
in writing. in 2000, i tabled with the intergroup on globalisation the first resolution calling on the commission to study the feasibility of a tax on speculative capital movements. it had not been voted on, by a few votes. ten years have passed, the g20, like several member states, no longer rule out the possibility of such a tax, and above all the financial crisis has reminded us of the damage that the volatility of financial markets can cause. that is why i welcome the broad adoption of the resolution on financial transaction taxes. it's a small step, but the message is clear. parliament called on the commission to finally address the issue and work on an implementation plan. such a tax would have the dual benefit of helping to stabilise markets and generate huge revenues to help developing countries finance their adaptation to climate change and the fight against poverty. we are opposed to it because it would only be effective if it were global, but we must start with it, as some countries are doing with the airline ticket tax. waiting will have no effect. we have to clear the way.
in writing. the resolution on acta, which i am one of the initiators of, is extremely symbolic because it was unanimous. it is a clear signal to the commission, which has been negotiating this agreement in the utmost secrecy for two years. parliament demands full transparency on the negotiations under way and respect for the treaties, which give it the right to information on an equal footing with the council. i am opposed to the acta negotiations as they are being conducted, both in terms of the method and in terms of what we know about the substance. we have many fears about the community acquis being called into question. beyond the risk of reintroducing the 'graduated' response, it is also the respect for citizens' fundamental rights, in terms of freedom of expression, privacy and data protection, as well as the principle of non-liability of internet service providers and web hosts that could be called into question. parliament has already shown its commitment to these principles and if the commission does not change its strategy, i will lead the fight against parliament's ratification of acta as we have already been able to do for the swift agreement.
in writing. despite the lisbon treaty and the codecision on international trade, the commission and the states are preventing a public debate on the anti-counterfeiting trade agreement (acac). this lack of transparency is creating a real suspicion which can only be mitigated by holding a public consultation and the european parliament. if the fight against counterfeiting is legitimate and necessary, the acac treaty would strengthen the power of copyright and copyrights. should we let the internet providers control the exchange of digital files, and impose sanctions against users (e.g. cutting off internet access)? the cost of such monitoring would be exorbitant for the access providers, and the checks complicated. moreover, internet hacking is not yet defined as a crime, either in european or international law. thus, a logic of systematic sanctioning on such a large scale is not legitimate, especially since access to the internet, in the name of the right to information, remains a fundamental freedom. the commission will have to make available to parliament a document setting out the negotiations and all the positions under discussion. otherwise, as with the swift agreement, parliament could reject this secretly negotiated text.
in writing. this draft agreement to combat counterfeiting and piracy, known as acta, may seem like a good idea, as much as the european economy and jobs suffer from these unfair practices in the ultra-barter world that you are imposing on us. but as always when there is something fundamentally harmful in an agreement negotiated by the commission, it is all done in secret. i am thinking of the blair house agreement which sacrificed european agriculture to the appetites of the american multinational agro-food companies. or the scandalous ami, the multilateral investment treaty, which sought to exempt multinational corporations from the laws of the countries in which they operated. fortunately, this one never came to be. here it is the acta "internet" component that is at issue: it is very much like introducing a monstrous worldwide "hadopi law"! customs could search mp3 players, phones and laptops of any citizen suspected of illegally downloading any file. internet service providers may be forced to remove their customers' login or provide information about them! this is unacceptable, and that is why we voted in favour of this resolution which calls for full transparency in the negotiations and threatens to bring the commission to justice if it refuses to do so.
in writing. i supported the resolution calling for full transparency from the european commission on the ongoing negotiations on the anti-counterfeiting trade agreement (acta) which are taking place behind closed doors. beyond the risk of reintroducing the 'graduated response', it is the respect for citizens' fundamental rights, in terms of freedom of expression, privacy and data protection, or the principle of non-responsibility of internet service providers and web hosts that could be called into question here. the european parliament, the voice of the european peoples, cannot therefore be left out of the negotiations and must receive the same information as that given to the council. this is a democratic requirement. finally, acta must not compromise access to generic medicines. in this context, considering that, to date, in view of the method and on the basis of the worrying rumours circulating as to its content, i can only express my support for a resolution critical of such an agreement.
in writing. the current scheme of generalised systems of preferences (gsp) is about to expire. i voted in favour of the resolution which aims in particular to involve parliament fully in its revision by 2012. this trade arrangement allows 176 developing countries and regions to benefit from preferential access to the european market in exchange for ratification of ilo conventions on social rights and un conventions on human rights. but its implementation is too weak. we therefore ask, before the review, for a report on the current state of ratification, the implementation of the conventions, an impact study of the effects of the gsp over the period 2006-2009, the inclusion of a condition for the effective implementation of 27 core un conventions and more transparent investigation procedures - including regular information to parliament. it is regrettable that an amendment calling for an investigation procedure in colombia into the numerous murders of trade unionists and the mass graves containing hundreds of bodies of people killed in the macarena region was not passed during this vote because of opposition from the right.

president of the european central bank. - the mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us in the last few years. i am pleased to be with you today for the debate on the resolution on the 2008 annual report of the european central bank. the european parliament has been a very active participant in the debate on the future of the european union. but it also gives me the opportunity to address the current situation at the end. as you know, mr president, the european central bank enjoys very close relations with parliament, which go well beyond the obligations laid down in the treaty. we have had a very fruitful dialogue over the years and i would like to say that the excellent reports we have heard from mr scicluna and mr giegold are a further testimony. today, in my report, i shall briefly review the economic developments observed in the past and the monetary policy measures taken by the central bank. i shall then address some points which have been raised in the motion for a resolution and say a few words on the current situation. first on the economic developments and monetary policy over the past year. in 2009, as was very eloquently said by mr scicluna, the european central bank was operating in an environment that future economic historians are likely to describe as the most difficult one for advanced economies since the second world war. following the profound intensification of the financial crisis in the autumn of 2008, 2009 started with a continued synchronised free fall in economic activity worldwide. until around april last year, economic activity was declining, month after month. during this period the trademark which was vital for maintaining confidence and it was the trademark of the ecb was the ability to take the immediate and exceptional decisions that were necessary while at the same time remaining inflexibly attached to our primary objective of maintaining price stability in the medium term. overall our non-standard monetary policy measures, which are known collectively as enhanced credit support, have served, we trust, the euro area economy well. they have supported the functioning of the money market, contributed to improving financing conditions and allowed for a better flow of credit to the real economy than could have been achieved through interest rate reductions alone. by and large, banks have been passing on the sharply lower key ecb interest rates to households and businesses. the guiding principle is that, to the extent that the situation returns to normal, keeping these measures in place for longer than required risks changing the behaviour of financial market participants in an undesirable manner, and we do not wish to spread dependency. this is why in december 2009, we began to gradually phase out some of our extraordinary liquidity measures, taking into account improvements in financial markets. in particular, we scaled back the number, frequency and maturity of longer-term refinancing operations. at the same time we have committed to maintaining fully accommodating liquidity support to the euro area banking system until at least october this year. the governing council is of the opinion that the current monetary policy stance is appropriate and that the continued firm anchoring of inflation expectations bodes well for price stability in the medium term. let me now turn to some of the issues you raise in the resolution and which were mentioned in the report. on the issues of accountability and transparency, we very much appreciate the regular dialogue with the european parliament and the constructive spirit with which this exchange is conducted. i therefore welcome the repeated support by the committee on economic and monetary affairs for our quarterly monetary dialogue. i think, as the rapporteur has said very eloquently, we are accountable to the european people, which means to parliament. we consider the ecb to be one of the world's most transparent central banks. our practice of holding a press conference immediately after the governing council meeting on monetary policy each month remains a pioneering initiative that has not yet been replicated by our major sister institutions. with the publication of our comprehensive introductory statement in real time, we explain policy decisions and their underlying rationale. during the crisis, as you know, we have further intensified our communication efforts and thereby helped to smooth financial market reactions, to build confidence and lay the foundations for recovery. you have also requested the views of the ecb on the establishment of a clearing house for instruments such as credit default swaps (cdss) within the euro area. i would like to say that the robustness of euro-denominated cds markets is of direct relevance for the eurosystem as regards control over its currency and financial stability in the euro area. central counterparty clearing is very important, not only for delivering transparency but also for diversifying and sharing risk exposures and reducing the incentives to take excessive risks. certain financial instruments which were introduced for hedging should not be misused for speculation. regulators should be able to undertake effective investigations into possible improper conduct, and there it seems to me that we are very much in line with parliament's concerns. let me say just a word on the outlook for emu during challenging times. an economic recovery is in progress, but this does not mean that the crisis is over. for one thing, we know that the pace of recovery will be uneven and we cannot rule out setbacks. for another, we are still facing numerous challenges regarding the reform of our financial system. finance must play a constructive role, and not a destructive one, in our economies. the litmus test for a constructive role is that finance serves the real economy. to ensure such a role, we still need to improve the functioning of financial systems considerably further. so far, a great deal of attention has been focused on the banking sector. effective reforms therefore have to look very closely at non-bank financial institutions and at the set-up and functioning of financial markets. we have to devise mechanisms and incentives to ensure that finance does not spiral out of control in the destructive way that it did just prior to the crisis. we have to contain systemic disruptions that lead to economic hardship for the people of europe. setting up the european systemic risk board, legislation for which is currently being considered by the parliament, is part of the correct response to this challenge. there are other challenges facing the european economy, and they are associated with public finances, as was again stressed by the rapporteur, and sovereign financial health. within europe's economic and monetary union, there is a clear allocation of responsibilities. with respect to that allocation of responsibilities, everyone can count on the commitment of the ecb to maintain price stability in the euro area as a whole over the medium term. based on our last projections for this year, we will have at the end of this year, after 12 years of the euro, inflation as an annual average of 1.95%. that is in line with our definition of price stability: less than 2%, but close to 2%. the ecb's commitment, the ecb's strategy and its track record are consistent. the smooth functioning of europe's economic and monetary union does not rest only on monetary union but also on economic union. policy-makers at the national level must keep public finances sound and their economies competitive. in the current circumstances, where europe faces pivotal decisions, it is more important than ever to recognise that a prosperous union requires determined action by all. monetary union in europe is far more, in my opinion, than a monetary arrangement. it is a union of shared destiny. (the speaker added in french and german: we share a destiny in common.) this destiny is for our common good, and it is the vision of our founding fathers. monetary union is not a matter of convenience. it is part of an overarching process of advancing the integration of the people in europe that began after the second world war. i believe we often play down the achievement that europe has attained. we are often too quick to criticize our institutions and processes. but they have generally worked well, even in the most difficult times. i trust that european institutions and processes have remained effective during the financial crisis. on this side of the atlantic we have avoided dramatic events that could have triggered a new intensification of the crisis, which began in the united states in september 2008. it is in this present context that i appreciate the commitment of euro area member states, made on the occasion of the last european council meeting, to take determined and coordinated action, if needed, to safeguard financial stability in the euro area. i would also like to take advantage of my presence before the european parliament to lay out what i have already mentioned at the hearing before the committee on economic and monetary affairs on monday. it is the intention of the ecb's governing council to keep the minimum credit threshold in the collateral framework at investment grade level (bbb-) beyond the end of 2010. in parallel, we will introduce, as of january 2011, a graded haircut schedule, which will continue to adequately protect the eurosystem. i will provide the technical details when reporting on the governing council decisions of our next meeting on 8 april. let me conclude. the introduction of the single currency just over a decade ago represents the greatest achievement, in my view, in the history of european integration to date a process that has ensured peace and prosperity in europe. the global financial crisis has brought fresh challenges to which we in europe have risen. our monetary union and our very close ties, inside the single market, with all eu member states' economies have prevented the crisis from being compounded by currency crises, as was the experience in the early 1990s. today, europe faces further pivotal decisions. our common task is to continue to ensure peace and prosperity, to make our union an even more attractive place to live and work in. for this we need strengthened surveillance as again was said by the rapporteurs, and strengthened cooperation. we also need to revive the sense of common purpose, the shared ideals that motivated our founding fathers. their endeavor was visionary and all that we see in today's world confirms their lucidity.
member of the commission. − mr president, first of all, i would like to thank you for the chance to discuss the 2009 annual statement on the euro area. when we prepared our annual statement, we knew that the selected issues would be topical. they might however have become somewhat too topical recently. let me congratulate both rapporteurs, edward scicluna and sven giegold, for their excellent reports. in order to respect the independence of the european central bank, i will focus on the giegold report, which makes a very substantive contribution to the current debate on economic coordination and economic governance within the euro area. in my view, the broad support the giegold report enjoyed within the committee on economic and monetary affairs is indeed a testimony to the relevance and balance of his approach and issues. i fully agree with mr trichet that the euro is not only a technical monetary arrangement but is rather the core political project of the european union, which must be defended and developed in this european spirit, not least today and tomorrow, as the european council is convening at a very critical moment. since 1999 the euro area has mostly been an area of economic stability. it has shielded our citizens from economic turbulences. however, since the end of 2008 the euro area has been hit hard by the global financial crisis. despite the economic recovery policies and strong fiscal stimulus, financial markets still remain volatile and the degree of uncertainty remains exceptionally high. recent waves in the market have seriously tested financial stability and economic governance in the euro area, especially in relation to greece. i would like to say that greece is now on track to meet the 4% target of deficit reduction this year, following the bold and convincing measures that the greek parliament decided earlier this month and which are now in force. this moment may indeed be a turning point in greek fiscal history and economic development. however, neither greece nor the eurozone are completely out of the woods yet as there are still concerns regarding financial stability in the euro area. therefore, the commission has strongly encouraged the euro area member states to take a political decision on a mechanism to ensure financial stability in the euro area as a whole, a mechanism which could be swiftly activated if needed, in conformity with the treaty and its bailout clause and without any automaticity built into this mechanism. on our side, i can assure you that the commission is ready to put such a european framework in place for coordinated and conditional assistance, which could be used if needed and if requested. we are working closely and intensively together with all euro area member states and the ecb in order to reach such a solution this week in the context of the european council. however, in addition to the immediate crisis management, we need to look at how similar situations can be avoided in the future so that we never again have cases similar to the greek case now. the greek crisis has demonstrated the need for enhanced economic governance. this was already recognised and the legal base provided in the lisbon treaty. therefore, we are currently preparing proposals for the implementation of article 136 of the lisbon treaty and the commission will make a proposal for enhanced economic policy coordination and reinforced country surveillance in the coming weeks. like you, mr giegold, in paragraph 28 we regret the lack of binding commitments among governments to enforce coordination in the euro area. therefore an integrated and forward-looking approach focused on policy action and clear operational arrangements is needed. first and foremost, we needed to prevent unsustainable public deficits and therefore we need to be better able to monitor the mid-term budgetary policies of the euro area member states. we need to be able to issue broader and more stringent recommendations to the member states to take corrective measures. i also count on your support in this matter. we can also make better use of existing instruments. it is possible for the council to address recommendations to a member state whose economic policies risk jeopardising the proper functioning of economic and monetary union. this has been used in the past, probably too rarely. with the new lisbon treaty, under article 21, the commission can issue similar early warnings directly to a member state. this is something we must do in order to help member states to address emerging economic problems at a much earlier stage. as i seem to be running on injury time, i will continue on macroeconomic imbalances in my concluding remarks. that is the second core element of reinforced economic governance. by and large, i share the views of the rapporteur in this regard. i just want to conclude by saying that the financial crisis has harshly demonstrated that the continuous economic growth of past decades cannot be taken for granted. today the worst may be over. the economic recovery is now in progress but it is still fragile and not self-sustaining. unemployment has not yet changed for the better. the same applies to the consolidation of public finances, which is a prerequisite for sustainable growth. no matter how important fiscal stimulus was for the economic recovery, the two years of the crisis have wiped out over 20 years of consolidation of public finances. these clouds will overshadow our economic landscape in the coming years. we must do our utmost to clear the sky and bring back growth. therefore this is indeed no time for business as usual. instead, this is time for a change in step to promote sustainable growth and job creation.
on behalf of the ppe group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, let me first congratulate and thank the rapporteur, mr giegold, who has done a very good job and has listened to the rapporteurs from the other groups. this report, which is the european parliament's response to the european commission's annual declaration on the euro area and public finances, is rich in analyses and proposals. of course, it is largely marked by the key element of 2009, the economic and financial crisis, which is undoubtedly the most serious crisis the european union has experienced since its creation. i take two main lessons from this crisis. on the one hand, economic and monetary union has shown its benefits. the euro, a stable common currency, has acted as a real monetary shield. membership of the euro area has enabled more than one country to avoid a depreciation of its national currency, which would have further aggravated the consequences of the crisis. the euro area has thus become more attractive, as the case of iceland shows. in addition, the active and flexible monetary policy pursued by the ecb, increasing its liquidity injections into credit institutions, has played a considerable role in keeping european banks afloat. the first lesson, then, is that while it is often said that europe was built on crises, it has shown that economic europe is both effective and necessary. the second lesson i draw from this is that we must strengthen european economic governance. today, the only real european economic policy is monetary. the coordination of budgetary policies is limited. the euro area, which, as the report reiterates, is intended to include all the member states of the european union, must have effective governance in all areas of economic policy. it must start with macroeconomic and financial surveillance, which we are working on in the european parliament. it must be conducted within the framework of the stability and growth pact as a genuine instrument of fiscal coordination. in this crisis period, the sharp fall in incomes, the fiscal incentives provided under the recovery plan and the operation of the economic stabilisers led to a deterioration in the budgetary balances of the member states. reducing public debt remains a fundamental commitment because it concerns the future of our children. let us be rigorous but let us also be inventive. let us think about a new european fiscal policy, let us think about eurobonds, let us be bold in european economic governance.
on behalf of the s&d group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the sven giegold report is of particular importance in the current macroeconomic debate. this report is all the more relevant since its author is a german member of parliament who wanted to draw the attention of europeans to the harmful effects on the euro area countries of the german strategy of reducing wage costs in a single currency. the german government is in fact about to drag the euro area and the entire european union into a widespread wage deflation with damaging macroeconomic consequences. in particular, in the absence of substantial structural funds and sufficient budgetary resources, and in the absence of the possibility of devaluation, states with current account deficits are condemned to reduce their wages and reduce the scope of their social protection systems in order to resist. this results firstly in a slowdown in domestic demand leading to negative growth as early as the second quarter of 2008, even before the outbreak of the liquidity crisis. secondly, there is an increase in private debt of households with low and medium incomes, whose purchasing power has stopped growing. their debt to buy homes was fuelled by the whole deregulated financial machine in spain, the uk and ireland, with the disastrous consequences seen in the subprime crisis. ladies and gentlemen, listening to the debates in committee, a significant number of members tend to forget the lessons of this crisis. this crisis is far from over. the current recovery is all the more fragile as europe continues to be in wage deflation and the commission, but also the president of the eurogroup and the president of the european central bank - in writing. animal welfare is an important issue. european regulations in this area must be applied rigorously, as mrs paulsen's report recommends. we must also ensure that the animal welfare standards imposed in the eu are applied reciprocally to products entering the european territory. our farmers and the european agri-food industry must not be penalised for incurring additional costs to meet eu requirements. animal welfare standards must coexist with european trade policy, with the protection of our jobs or with the practice of hunting activities which allow the regulation of wildlife which is essential for the balance of biodiversity. i also have reservations about the creation of a european network of reference centres for animal welfare. as rapporteur on the 2008 discharge for the eu decentralised agencies, i am well aware of the problem of the creation of agencies, which unfortunately lacks overall coherence. this issue, which is being addressed by the interinstitutional working group on agencies, needs to be resolved before considering the creation of new agencies.
the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, the report i am presenting to parliament is an attempt to explain that agriculture has a place and a role to play in the fight against global warming. nature this week - and volcanoes in particular - reminds us that they can have a major impact on human activities and the climate. but it still requires that men, and europe in particular, take responsibility for combating what is called global warming. my report tries to show that agriculture can continue to reduce its carbon emissions, reduce its fossil fuel consumption and, above all, on the other hand, participate very actively in carbon sequestration in order to achieve, at the global level, a lower proportion of carbon emissions and a higher proportion of carbon sequestered and sequestered. this report tries to show that in agriculture we should move from a compartmentalized approach which consists of opening up a directive on soils, water, pesticides, whatever else, whenever we have a problem, to try to tackle the agricultural question with the ambition of dealing with it in a comprehensive, systemic way. in this approach, we must be able to find ways of ensuring that agriculture, as i said earlier, not only reduces its energy consumption, but at the same time participates very actively in carbon sequestration. in particular, the role of photosynthesis, biomass and, above all, what i am particularly fond of, also related to soils, the capacity of european soils to store organic carbon. i think that the path i am opening up in this report, which i hope will be followed in the vote in plenary in brussels, must enable european agriculture to enter a phase of sustainability, to ensure an ecological transition to agriculture that would put it ahead of a number of other continents or other agriculture to ensure that it is capable of being economically efficient, ecologically efficient and, from that point on, socially efficient. this report therefore deals with a particular issue, the fight against global warming and agriculture, but it is intended -
