in writing. the purpose of this draft regulation is to harmonise the rules on the placing on the market of novel foods in the union. the first objective is to ensure a high level of protection of human life and health and animal health and welfare, while being consistent with the transparency and efficient functioning of the internal market and the need to stimulate innovation in the agri-food industry. i supported this report, even though i opposed several amendments tabled in plenary: amendment no 11, which states that 'foodstuffs produced from cloned animals or their descendants should therefore not be included in the union list' and amendment no 14, which concerns the scope and aims to exclude animals produced from cloned animals or their descendants. the question here is not whether or not to approve the placing on the market of food derived from cloned animals and their offspring, but to ask the european commission for a specific proposal on the subject, without prejudice to whether or not to ban it.
in writing. - i voted for amendment no 37 to the report on 'new foods'. i support the proposal to ask the european commission to initiate legislative measures to ban the placing on the market of products derived from cloned animals. according to the european food safety authority, the production of food from cloned animals is not currently justified on ethical grounds: cloned animals have serious health problems, most of them dying in the first days or weeks of life. veterinarians decided to euthanize dolly the sheep, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell, because she suffered from severe health problems. this case has brought up the implications of animal cloning. the citizens of the european union do not want to clone animals for food. according to a survey by the european commission, 84% of citizens believe that the long-term effects of eating food from cloned animals are not sufficiently known. there are also concerns about the possible side effects of eating these foods. another argument against cloning animals for food is that the european market is sufficiently supplied with food.
in writing. in the context of this report, meps from the democratic movement voted in favour of an amendment which would make it compulsory for food from animals fed with genetically modified organisms to bear a label informing the consumer of the use of gmos. unfortunately, this amendment did not obtain a qualified majority, so we will have to come back to it with the future major reform of the common agricultural policy. another key point of debate was cloned animals, their offspring and the food they produce. the council and the commission wanted to include the descendants of cloned animals in the category of 'new foods', a position that was clearly rejected by the meps from the democratic movement, as well as by the majority of parliamentarians. at present, there is no legislation to allow or disallow products derived from cloned animals (e.g. milk or meat). meps therefore called for legislation expressly banning food from cloned animals and their offspring, with a moratorium on their sale. thanks to this vote, dolly won't end up on your plate.
in writing. the european parliament is called upon to give its opinion on the draft legislative resolution tabled by kartika tamara liotard on 'new foods'. new foods, food supplements, may be of plant or animal origin, or may be the result of scientific and technological research. these are ingredients or foods that have been negligible or non-existent in consumption up to now. however, the european union still legislates. food is the basis of life; changing what humans have known for millennia in favor of concessions to the big food industries is risky. animal cloning for food production or gmos are on the agenda, in ambush. it is not for the european union to impose these novel foods and the legislation relating to them in the member states. such a decision constitutes a violation of national sovereignty and i reiterate my opposition to this report.
in writing. just as i was outraged by the european commission's decision earlier this year to allow the use of gmos in europe, i strongly opposed the commission's proposal on 'new foods' on two points, namely cloned animals and the use of nanotechnologies. so i voted, of course, against the authorization of food products derived from clones and in favour of a moratorium on the sale and marketing of food products modified by nanotechnology. the commission and the council did not want a specific regulation for these two types of food, but this is essential: in both cases, until it is proved that it is harmless, until the health risks have been ruled out, these products should not be authorized. these issues need further study, as they concern food safety and food protection for european citizens, but also ethical issues.
in writing. while the debate on novel foods is likely to be a long and contentious one, i am pleased that the european parliament has maintained its first reading position at second reading, despite the strong reluctance of the council and the commission. i therefore voted in favour of this report for a simple reason: apart from my ethical objections to industrial production from cloned animals, i do not want these food products to end up on the table of european consumers, given the ongoing doubts about the safety of cloned meat. in this connection, i voted in favour of a separate legislative proposal, expressly banning food derived from cloned animals and their offspring. in the same spirit of caution, i have also supported a moratorium on the marketing of nanotechnology products until a risk assessment has been carried out, and a clear labelling of nano-ingredients. i regret, however, that the amendment calling for mandatory labelling of food products from animals fed gmos has been rejected.
in writing. political leaders cannot accept risk to the health of our citizens and our ecosystem. until the safety of every cloning technique and other genetic modification is proven, we will need to be safe from anything that comes out of it in any generation.
in writing. the liotard report on novel foods reflects parliament's concerns about food produced from cloned animals and the use of nanotechnologies. i share these concerns and have therefore supported him. there is currently no community legislation to allow or prohibit dairy products and meat from cloned animals, whereas we have been calling for appropriate legislation on this subject at european level for years. in the meantime, we propose to expressly ban food derived from cloned animals and their offspring. on the question of foodstuffs modified by nanotechnology (any ingredient in the form of nanomaterial or any foodstuff produced by a means of production using nanotechnology), i am in favour of the precautionary principle and therefore of a moratorium as long as the health risks are not eliminated. i therefore welcome the signal sent by parliament today, even if i consider it a mistake to reject amendment no 76 calling for the labelling of foodstuffs from gm-raised animals, which i supported: i believe that, in the context of a policy of transparency in labelling and consumer accountability, this measure is desirable at european level, given the sensitivity of the subject.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report by my colleague, kartika liotard (gue/ngl/netherlands), on the rules for the marketing authorisation of novel foods. the regulation calls for a ban on the sale of foodstuffs derived from cloned animals. this is urgent, as the cloning technique is not yet mastered. today, more than half of the cloned animals die prematurely, suffer deformities and other health problems. food from such clones should therefore not be on the plate of our fellow citizens. it also provides a framework for the testing and evaluation of nanomaterials. research is very recent in this area and the steps in the large-scale marketing of such products should not be burnt. consumer safety must therefore be given priority. i regret, however, that the european parliament has rejected some of kartika liotard's proposals, in particular on the assimilation of certain products (additives, flavourings, etc.) to foodstuffs, the publication of european studies in this field or labelling, in particular that of products from animals fed gmos.
in writing. there are currently too many directives on industrial emissions in the european union, as there are seven. this report therefore responds to an urgent need to rationalise european legislation by bringing together all the directives on industrial emissions in a single text. in addition, installations are a central element in the prevention and reduction of pollution from industrial emissions. that is why i supported the khramer report. it has taken environmental issues into account by strengthening the role of sectoral reference documents on best available techniques in determining the operating conditions of installations, by strengthening the provisions on closure and rehabilitation of sites, etc. this text has been the subject of long negotiations and it seems to me that the compromise is finally very satisfactory for our fellow europeans. that's why i supported him.
in writing. the highly controversial recasting into a single text of the seven directives which regulated industrial emissions in europe has finally been adopted, and we can welcome this vote. the aim is to minimise the overall harmful effects of most industrial activities within the eu, i.e. emissions of potential pollutants into air, water, soil and waste. the final agreement reached goes further. it takes up the key points of the position we have been defending in the committee on the environment for several months, which aimed to make this text an ambitious but realistic piece of legislation, in line with the problems of our territories. the agreement strengthens the provisions on environmental protection, but gives the member states some flexibility which we have fought for with a framework for large combustion plants. in this time of crisis we need a strong european environmental policy, but one which will not bring our industry to its knees. industrial strategy and policy should no longer be taboo concepts in brussels: let us simply look at what our competitors are doing in third countries!
in writing. the proposal we are voting on updates, in a single text, seven existing laws on industrial emissions, including the important directives on large combustion plants and on integrated pollution prevention and control (the famous ippc, which covers some 52 000 industrial and agricultural plants - from refineries to pig farms - with a high pollution potential). i welcome the fact that after two years of difficult negotiations a compromise was finally reached at the third trilogue in june. as in all compromises, there are concessions and advances, but overall the european parliament has fought for greater clarity and fairness in environmental requirements: the text clearly makes major progress on several key points (notably on air quality, optimisation of environmental performance, and strengthening of member states' obligations in the area of plant monitoring). finally, i note with satisfaction the provision for the commission to draw up, before the end of 2011, a legislative proposal to amend the authorisation thresholds for poultry species, which will include the specific case of quails, which is a sensitive subject in my constituency.
in writing. the report aims to reduce the placing on the internal market of wood or derived products from illegal harvesting. i supported him in the vote because he found a satisfactory principle for protecting european consumers and manufacturers, the principle of 'duty of due diligence'. this principle provides for measures and procedures to enable operators to trace timber and derived products, to have access to information on compliance with applicable legislation and to manage the risk of placing illegally harvested timber and derived products on the internal market.
in writing. the prohibition of the import of illegal timber is a necessity, particularly in the context of the fight against global warming. this ban, which is expected to cover 20 to 40% of timber imported into europe, will make a real breakthrough in the fight against deforestation. it will lead to a very significant reduction in co2 emissions into the atmosphere and help protect animal and plant species that are currently endangered. this measure will also improve the living conditions of local communities dependent on the forest and, more generally, of the entire population of the countries concerned. by making illegal exploitation more difficult, in particular by imposing traceability on importers, and by encouraging legal exploitation and therefore the payment of taxes in the country of production, the european union is supporting the states concerned in their fight against tax evasion, which will enable them to have more resources at their disposal, which they can put at the service of the people.
in writing. 20% of the wood and wood products that reach the eu are of illegal origin, and illegal logging is a powerful driver of deforestation, which is increasing by almost 13 million hectares each year and leading to a dramatic depletion of natural resources and biodiversity. in the face of this, parliament has just decided to refuse the importation of illegally harvested timber into the european area, and i welcome this decision which represents a major international step forward: the european union is thus finally taking its responsibilities in terms of international trade and the fight against deforestation.
in writing. i supported this second reading agreement because we must avoid any bureaucratic and costly processes to safeguard the future of wood, by effectively fighting illegal timber in europe. we must strengthen our control of imports to put a stop to deforestation once and for all. the efforts of operators and public authorities must be concentrated on the closest link to the harvesting of wood, namely the first marketing on community territory. it would have been irresponsible to penalise our european publishers by asking them to prove the origin of the paper used by the printers for their books. it is impossible to determine the origin of the wood used in the paper.
in writing. i voted in favour of this draft regulation laying down the obligations of operators marketing wood and wood products on the european market. i welcome the ban on the placing on the european internal market of illegally harvested timber. this decision is essential in the fight against illegal deforestation linked to the exploitation of exotic wood for western consumers. it is also a significant step in the fight against global warming. the regulation provides significant guarantees in terms of firmness, deterrence and harmonisation of member states' legislation. this is a necessary step in the effective fight against this illegal trade in the eu. it will help to preserve the future of wood materials. i therefore welcome the very soon entry into force of this new regulation, which proves that in certain areas the european union can play a positive role if its member states apply this legislation correctly.
in writing. the report aims to establish a sound, independent and accountable supervisory system which should form the basis of european action in relation to financial markets. this is a european but also a global commitment, as the g20 committed to 'acting to establish a more robust and globally consistent framework for the future supervision and regulation of the financial sector, which is capable of fostering sustainable growth and meeting the needs of businesses and citizens' (g20 summit, 2 april 2009 in london). the current financial and economic crisis has revealed the persistence of imbalances between financial globalisation, eu financial integration and national supervisory arrangements, which we now need to address. i therefore committed myself, in voting in favour of this report, to moving towards a more integrated supervisory structure, always with a view to an integrated single market in financial markets. the ball is now in the council's court, which must also move towards a genuine european financial surveillance.
in writing. all the reports we were called upon to vote on under the 'supervision' package have the same flaw. if they strengthen the surveillance of financial actors, banks, insurance companies, funds, etc., which we can only approve, they do not change anything about what is being monitored. they do not address the root of the problem: the financial, globalized capitalist system. these same actors will be able to continue to create complex products, to securitize debts and to exchange them, in short, to carry out a financial activity totally disconnected from the real production of wealth ... instead of banning a number of assets with perverse fundamentals which, far from improving the liquidity available to economic activity, only create artificial and predatory profit, they are "monitored" and "regulated". what a deal! the lamfalussy procedure is hailed here as the jewel of virtue. but it must be said that, in view of the immorality, even cynicism, of the behaviour of certain financial institutions and their managers, to give them such power to intervene in the regulations which concern them is something unhealthy, and even deeply perverse.
in writing. the purpose of this draft regulation is to establish a european financial markets authority. this authority will be one of the three new ones created to set up a new supervisory framework. this will help to improve the effectiveness of supervision and regulation and to better identify risks in the financial system. as part of my overall support for the financial supervision package, i support the creation of such an authority. i therefore voted in favour of this report which, while supporting the european commission's proposal for a regulation, states that the authority's mediation role, which is essential for an effective and accountable supervisory framework, will nevertheless need to be better defined and improved.
in writing. this is a proposal for a regulation on the macroprudential supervision of the financial system, establishing a european systemic risk board. i strongly support the financial supervision package as adopted by the parliament's committee on economic and monetary affairs. the aim of this body of legislation is multifaceted, but two main ones can be identified: stable financing of the economy for sustainable growth and jobs, and the desire to safeguard the unity of the european market. i therefore voted in favour of this report, which has provided for consistency between macroprudential and microprudential supervision and will thus enable the european union to have stable, transparent and consistent authorities and committees for the management of our european and global financial system.
in writing. the european systemic risk board (esrb) is nothing but a body of the reigning euro-liberalism and a prototype of the bypass of democracy. its general council will be composed of members of the ecb, the commission and the national central banks, but will not include any members of parliament. the esrb will never warn us of the dangers of the policies it advocates. it is therefore harmful, as is the proposal in this report, to allow the esrb to work closely with the imf and the g20. i am voting against this text.
in writing. i have clearly supported this report, which aims to create a european banking authority and to set up a settlement mechanism for future crises, in order to avoid european citizens having to bear the consequences of a collapse of the financial system. i particularly appreciate the european approach taken by our rapporteur. it is clearly in favour of a so-called 'european' option which would involve giving colleges of supervisors the possibility of setting binding standards where agreement cannot be reached at national level. in addition, the creation of a european fund pre-financed by financial institutions is envisaged, the aim being to protect depositors and to help institutions in difficulty when their bankruptcy risks destabilising the whole system. finally, i very much appreciate the support that the rapporteur wants to give to small and mediumsized enterprises, which are often too underrepresented in the banking sector. the report therefore provides that representatives of small and medium-sized enterprise organisations will sit on the banking stakeholder group and elect two members of the board of supervisors.
in writing. as part of the financial supervision package, this draft regulation aims to establish a european insurance and occupational pensions authority. the authority complements the supervisory framework, alongside the european banking authority and the european securities and markets authority. i believe that the european parliament must make a clear statement in favour of integrated supervision at european level and that it is now up to the council to do the same.
in writing. first of all, it should be noted that the lack of capital in the banking system was a central factor in the crisis, hence the importance of implementing an increase in capital. i therefore voted in favour of this report. the latter is firmly opposed to the idea of privatising profits and nationalising losses, or of passing them on to society as a whole. the present system, in particular the remuneration policy in the banking system, encourages high risk taking. excessive bonuses have led to the short-term pursuit of profit at the expense of the medium- and long-term stability of the financial system. for example, the report makes a good point about the need for remuneration to be based on incentive systems and not on guarantees given to employees, regardless of the profits and losses made. in addition, it aims to establish a remuneration committee within the company to improve transparency and information and to defend long-term interests.
in writing. the legislation proposed today is, in general, to strengthen capital requirements in line with the risks taken by financial institutions, and to regulate bonuses and other golden parachutes. i'm sorry it doesn't go far enough. it does not, for example, go so far as to cap these bonuses, to require that they not be the main part of wages or to ban certain so-called 'toxic' products. this legislation does not go far enough, but it is moving in the right direction. and it is a pity that many of the financial sector reforms in the european union, which are presented as urgent and indispensable, are being delayed for sometimes political reasons. another concern is that it is very good to impose new and stricter rules. but will this be enough to put finance back at the service of the economy? nothing is less certain. the banks were quick to repay the state aid, without fulfilling their credit obligations to companies and individuals, so that they could pay out exceptional bonuses. speculation is at its highest, above all, since it is known that the taxpayer will pay whatever happens. it's not just the rules that need to change, it's the system itself.
in writing. i voted for the mccarthy report on bankers' pay because the excessive pursuit of short-term profits by an oversized financial sector has deeply destabilised the financial sector and contributed to the crisis. the text, adopted by an overwhelming majority in the european parliament, caps variable remuneration and allows the deferral of up to 70% of the trader bonus to take account of the bank's long-term interests. the text thus has a twofold objective: to stabilise the financial sector and to put it back at the service of long-term investment.
in writing. the mccarthy report aims to set a framework for the remuneration of traders and to establish new rules on the capital of banks. this is just another attempt to regulate the banks, and the regulations have not been effective. these measures are merely a form of publicity. adding more regulation will not be a lifesaver, as banks will once again hijack regulation. the overcompensation of traders can only be stopped if trading on the capital of banks is prohibited. this requires the separation of banking activity into deposit banking and investment banking, with the former being prohibited from lending to the latter. the size of the largest financial institutions must be reduced to prevent abuse of a dominant position. banks must be subject to the 100% money rule; they could therefore only lend what they owned. the increase in the money supply must be returned to the state and the state must refrain from bailing out banks in the event of a risk of bankruptcy. only then will bankers be responsible and will they seriously assess the risks they take.
in writing. i abstained on the so-called "financial supervision" package. despite some small measures to manage the situation, the proposed responses are not up to the current crisis and would be even less able to prevent new ones. it is not enough to create new bodies to regulate the financial sector. the composition of the general council of the european systemic risk board (esrb), with only representatives of the ecb, the commission and the national central banks, without any parliamentarians, speaks for itself, especially as this new body should work in close collaboration with the imf and the g20 and without any exchange with the committee of the regions or the social partners. instead of strengthening a stability pact that is no longer anything but an austerity pact, it is time to challenge it, to effectively control the financial markets and the ecb, and to implement new economic and social policies geared to job creation and the fight against poverty. the public debt crisis is a sign of the failure of current policies. it's time to learn the lessons.
in writing. i voted in favour of this report because it affirms several principles to which i am committed, including the fact that the answers to banking difficulties should not be borne by the taxpayer but should first be addressed by the banking sector. trust is also a principle that this report aims to consolidate; trust for financial markets in the member states, but also mutual trust between the 27 member states. finally, through this report i supported initiatives already undertaken such as the development of mandatory contingency plans by each institution within colleges of supervisors and the choice of a stability fund (privately funded and publicly managed) instead of a bank levy.
in writing. the main aim of mrs ferreira's report is not to manage crises effectively, but to prevent them from being solved by states. fortunately, however, governments have taken matters into their own hands quickly, without waiting for the commission to begin to wake up, entangled in its bureaucratic dogmas, focused on competition and its hatred of subsidies, stunned by its inability to see the crisis coming, although it has been predictable for a year. the european institutions were the most useless thing in the emergency. the heads of state or government had the elegance to drag mr barroso along at the important meetings. but, if you don't mind me saying, the decisions were made at the intergovernmental level. i am not saying that the decisions taken by the states were perfect: they had the merit of being taken and of being taken quickly. i am sure that the provisions of the report will not be able to make us forget the shortcomings of the past, nor will they guarantee efficiency in the future.
in writing. to avoid economic crises in the future and thus to promote growth potential and macroeconomic rebalancing within the european union, progress in fiscal and structural policies in the individual member states is essential. i therefore voted in favour of this motion for a resolution because it correctly defines the issues and the ways forward for improving the surveillance framework. the future supervisory framework should therefore ensure sustainable public finances and economic growth, competitiveness, social cohesion and the reduction of trade imbalances. to do this, we must tackle the structural problems facing the european union. the resolution therefore seeks to address the problem of internal imbalances and unsustainable debt and to address the significant disparities in competitiveness between member states.
in writing. i did not vote for the resolution on the european financial stabilisation mechanism. this mechanism, created out of thin air and in an emergency last may at the height of the greek bond crisis, was a major breakthrough in the economic governance of the euro area. but on this question our parliament has shown a serious lack of vision. several key amendments were rejected, including the most important one, which i regard as the most important, namely the one calling for the sustainability of this system through the creation of a european monetary fund, the first step towards a european bond market which i have already repeatedly called for. i am also surprised that this parliament has refused to acknowledge the positive role played by the ecb throughout this period, particularly in its decision to buy sovereign debt on the secondary market, which helped to relax the bond market. in the end, this resolution, which has no legislative scope, gives a very timid image of our parliament, while the commission, together with the council, is working on the contrary to maintain in the long term this mechanism which is essential for the stability of the euro.
in writing. this report makes good sense on at least one point: you do not solve a debt crisis by adding new debts to it. but the financial stability mechanism devised by the council and endorsed in this report makes the granting of new european loans conditional on the implementation of economic and financial reforms in line with the policies that created this crisis. so this report is absurd. it also welcomed the austerity plans put in place and the commission's proposals on ex ante control of national budgets and the strengthening of sanctions in the event of non-application of the stability and growth pact. the report therefore proposes to violate the sovereignty of peoples and nations. the role of parliamentarians is to defend the interests of the people, not those of the fallen elites. i am voting against this text.

president of the council. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank you for inviting me to this debate, which i consider to be extremely important. it's good that we can have it on risk and safety, regulation of offshore oil exploitation. after the disaster we have seen in the gulf of mexico, the situation obviously cannot leave us indifferent when we think of the victims, when we also think of the extremely serious, and probably sometimes irreparable, damage to the environment that has been caused in this region, and we have a duty to draw all the conclusions now in order to prevent a disaster of this kind from occurring in europe. the situation in europe is not the same, as we know. the conditions for exploitation are already stricter. we're drilling less offshore, at depths that are infinitely less than what we were dealing with in the gulf of mexico accident. nevertheless, as the saying goes, one can never be too careful, and we are right to consider a more preventive policy. i would also like to commend the commission for its dynamism and proactivity, which on 11 may took the initiative of consulting and questioning the industry and which will resume - commissioner oettinger will tell you in more detail and better than i - its consultations on 14 july. i am told that a debate was held in your chamber on 18 may. the council has also taken up the subject, and we had a first debate with the commission at our last energy council on 31 may. the first informal contacts with the commission suggest that we could return to this at the informal council in september, to ensure that the pressure on this matter is not relaxed. we have also discussed these issues at the various bilateral meetings we have had, no later than 28 june, with the opec countries. the question now is whether more legislation is needed in this area, where there are already a number of important rules on the safety of operating platforms, the safety of workers, etc. we already have, of course, the european maritime safety agency and civil protection mechanisms. do we need more? do we need to tighten these rules further? this is the question we will have to ask ourselves as soon as the commission has completed its analysis. i have already told you, the commissioner - and he will tell you again, better than i - is continuing his analysis of legislation, consulting the member states and the industry. i would simply like to make a plea on behalf of the council that the commission should widen its contacts and that it should have contacts with other types of experts, academic experts, for example, so as to bring as many points of view as possible together around the table. the idea is that, on the basis of this comprehensive analysis - which i hope will be forthcoming soon - we can consider - as a first step - the revision of the regulation on the european maritime safety agency - a strengthening of the european regulatory and legislative arsenal in this field. we will also have to consider not only the platforms that are still in operation today but also those that are no longer in operation and will have to be dismantled at some point. this is also a question of major risks and possible risks on the ecological level and naturally raises the question of financial responsibility and the technical conditions for this dismantling. that is the set of questions that the council would like us to debate. i would like to assure you, madam president, ladies and gentlemen, that the belgian presidency is determined to ensure that this matter is followed up with great care and that at no time can the attention we have begun to give it be slackened.

the ministries and the specialised agencies. i want to discuss with them the possibilities and the need to bring european standards up to a uniform european level and to the highest possible level. today i want to address five key points where i believe action is needed, from prevention to remediation to liability. firstly, the new drilling. they know that the approval and examination of applications for new drilling rigs, for new drilling opportunities, is the responsibility of our member states. my clear advice to member states today is that i would not recommend, but would postpone, authorizations for new drilling, particularly for extreme drilling, at this stage. in fact, this may be a moratorium. it's not a bad thing. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. our governments will and must ensure that industry provides all safety and prevention measures at the highest possible level. this is particularly true in extreme climatic and geophysical conditions. secondly, it is a question of the level of prevention and of strengthening control. we're looking at all the contingency plans, we need to look at best practice, where we can learn from each other; the approval procedures shall include critical responsiveness. the financial background must also be taken into account, so that the responsibility for damage, i.e. the polluter principle, is not only theoretical but can actually be borne. in addition to the liability of the person responsible for the accident, whether or not the fault is attributable to him, it is also possible to examine whether insurance solutions, compulsory insurance solutions or even pre-insurance solutions are useful. i think the usual division of labour between national and eu authorities is not really satisfactory. we need a new model, more synergies and more efficient cooperation, perhaps even a system of auditing the of auditors and a common audit standard should be introduced in addition. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rules are applied. i want to ensure that europe has the highest safety standards and the highest legislation in a global comparison. this is acceptable because the damage, including the economic damage, clearly outweighs the cost of preventing an want to develop a debate worldwide that makes comparable environmental disasters impossible in any region of the world, first of all in the marine region within our reach, but in the future worldwide. the council, to the council of ministers, to the european council and to parliament. i am counting on your expertise, your interest and your cooperation.
member of the commission. − madam president, i am in full agreement with the statement of my colleague, mr oettinger. let me add just a few points. let me first remind you of an obvious fact which, however, has not been mentioned sufficiently these last few days. this dramatic accident happened at sea. what does that mean? its consequences are multiple. beyond the loss of lives, we had an unprecedented ecological disaster that affects the marine and coastal ecosystems, an economic and social catastrophe for tourism, for the fishing industry, as well as many other maritime and coastal activities. as commissioner oettinger said before me, it is a moment for us to analyse existing legislation, in order to check if it provides complete coverage for risk management and prevention. we also have to demand guarantees from oil companies, for full safety, referring to all their activities. this is very important. full safety in all their activities and full application of the polluter-pays principle . referring especially to my portfolio, if we have a situation where european fisheries become directly affected by a spill, i, as the commissioner in charge, will take the necessary steps to mitigate the impact on fishermen and their communities as far as possible and adequate. but i think that now is above all the moment to question ourselves on our addiction to oil and to look forward towards better management of the oceans and seas. this dependence on oil clearly comes at a price, which a large part of the population and of maritime stakeholders is no longer willing to pay. i am well informed about this. so we have to understand that there is great potential for future energy from the oceans. we need to put more emphasis on renewable ocean energy – not only offshore wind energy, this is obvious, but i am not only referring to this. i am referring also to sea energy, for example energy coming from waves, tides, the exploitation of algae or thermal sea potential. this energy is cleaner and will help us to achieve our climate-action targets and the diversification of energy sources. it also offers a huge potential for highly qualified new employment in maritime sectors and coastal regions. europe is the maritime continent par excellence and we should take the lead in the development of sustainable marine energy sources. we need the tools for a prevention policy as mr oettinger said but, at the same time, we need to allow balanced and sustainable exploitation of the marine sources. how can we achieve this? integrated maritime special planning can give us this opportunity. it is the key instrument in reconciling conflicting interests in the issue of this space. it can anticipate future challenges and operational skills. equally, our knowledge of the deep sea is dramatically poor and we have to understand this. today, for example, nobody can say for sure whether the spill will reach european shores, which creates justified concerns for us. we clearly need to better understand the deep sea. this means that we need to increase our research activities and to develop our maritime surveillance capacities in terms of satellites and equipment in general and with regard to data gathering and modelling. we are also seeing the need for international cooperation and understanding. so far, only the united states is directly affected but i think it is fair to say that this disaster is also a lesson in humility. we need to share experiences, best practice in governance and disaster response. in conclusion, the integrated maritime policy of the european union will help the commission’s ongoing work and prepare the ground for a secured, balanced and sustainable use of the oceans.

the rapporteur. - mr president, madam commissioner, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, one of the strong points of this report is the need to achieve the necessary coherence between the common commercial policy and the common fisheries policy. in this context, we can only be pleased to see the commissioner for fisheries, maria damanaki, our usual interlocutor, and the commissioner for trade, karel de gucht, on the commission's benches today. two commissioners for one report, what an honor! i would like to say that i am surprised and flattered by the commission's unusual double representation. let us return to the report itself. imports of fishery and aquaculture products from third countries account for more than 60% of community consumption. this very worrying level of import dependence in the european union is the result of a twofold phenomenon: on the one hand, a decline in community production and, on the other hand, an ever greater opening of the community market to imports, through the trade policies pursued by the commission over the last ten years. these developments are creating difficulties for community fishermen who, paradoxically, find it difficult to sell their catches at sufficiently remunerative prices, while the supply is lower than the demand for most species. european fishermen accept the environmental, social and health constraints imposed on them, but they are bitter about the fact that they do not apply in the same way to products imported en masse from third countries. what is at stake here is simply the survival of an economically viable european fisheries sector, providing jobs throughout the sector, providing safe and good quality food and contributing to the maintenance of the cultural identity of our coastal regions. the survival of european fisheries is not negotiable. we are essentially asking for: first, that the european union maintain significant tariff protection for fishery and aquaculture products, which allows the value of the preferences granted to certain third countries, particularly developing countries, to be maintained, and for the wto mechanisms to ensure the supply of our processing industry to be effective. we must remove these products from the real swiss-style tariff mills by requiring them to be treated as sensitive products. secondly, the trade preferences granted to certain third countries must be conditional on compliance with strict environmental, social and health standards, which is a minimum. thirdly, we are asking for the transfer of the main responsibility for conducting trade negotiations on fishery and aquaculture products from the commissioner for trade to the commissioner for fisheries. this will allow better account to be taken of the specific nature of fishery and aquaculture products. i think this is a particularly good time to review the terms of this fundamental debate. we are indeed on the eve of a major reform of the cfp. on the other hand, we see a deadlock in the doha round of the wto, which allows us to reconsider some inappropriate concessions that the commission was about to make on behalf of the european union. moreover, at the initiative of commissioner de gucht, who is here, the european commission has just opened a public consultation period with a view to formulating new guidelines for the common commercial policy, in the context of the europe 2020 strategy. the european parliament is now a co-decision-maker in both trade and fisheries policy, and it is keen to make its voice heard and its views respected in these matters. i believe that this will begin with the commission and the council taking the recommendations contained in this report seriously into account. in any case, we shall be very vigilant in the months ahead and i personally intend to continue to work on these issues.
member of the commission. − mr president, first of all i would like to thank mr cadec and the ep committees that have sponsored this own-initiative report. you have regretted that the green paper on the cfp reform did not pay enough attention to the issues you raise here. my objective today is to reassure you that the commission is committed to the work, taking into full account all policies that would have an impact on the cfp reform. as i have already stated, the purpose of the reform is to turn around the negative spiral we are in now. we have a fisheries sector that is neither ecologically sustainable nor economically performing well. we need robust fisheries that ensure sustainable exploitation of the resources while allowing our fishermen, their families and the communities involved to make a decent living from their activities. we need fisheries which are ready to meet the challenges of the market: both national and international, and both currently and for the future. i hear your concerns about unfair competition from third countries and the absence of a level playing field in terms of social conditions, environmental and sustainability requirements and health protection laws. let me tell you that this same concern was voiced by all the member states which took the floor at the last agriculture and fisheries council. so here we need an answer. while we are changing the rules for european fisheries in the context of our cfp reform, one of the biggest challenges we will have will be precisely to do our best in order to secure a level playing field for all products placed on the eu market. in this respect, for instance, we should all work together to fully and effectively implement our legislation against illegal, unregulated and unreported fishing. i would also like to say that we remain committed to promoting the respect of all international principles and instruments of good maritime and fishery governance by our partners, as well as their responsible behaviour in terms of environmental protection and social conditions. i strongly support your call for an increased coherence of our policies. we need to work together with a global and integrated vision. two thirds of the fish consumed in europe, as we have already mentioned, are already imported in order to ensure a steady supply of raw material to our processing industry and fair prices to consumers. yet one third of the eu market is still supplied by an eu sector that represents jobs and this part of the social fabric of many regions in europe. so, while we are in the middle of a serious reform of our common fisheries policy, eu trade policy should continue to take into account the complex nature of the eu’s fishing sector and its economic and social realities. i look forward to working closely together with my colleague mr de gucht in order to secure the necessary time for the adjustments that are needed, taking into account the pace of the ongoing cfp reform. with reference to wto negotiations, we are paying particular attention to the ongoing discussions on subsidies. it is our view that we should always be able to support environmentally friendly and innovation-oriented initiatives of our member states. concerning the revision of the market policy, i agree with the draft report that the new market policy of the cfp should revisit the instruments of the current common market organisation. the revision should aim at strengthening producer organisations in their ability to better link the supply to demand in terms of quality and volumes. it shall also support market supply and stability and review provisions of marketing standards and information to consumers. this brings us to labelling. consumers want to know more about the seafood they buy. they want to know where the fish was caught or raised; also they want to know whether the products respect the environment and whether they have been fished sustainably. the commission is ready to work on legislative initiatives aiming at giving consumers the information they need. finally, a word on aquaculture. the commission is fully committed to achieving the objectives of the strategy for the sustainable development of aquaculture, as we have already discussed in the ep report. we also share the view that developing aquaculture in the eu can lead to reduced dependence on imports and better respond to constantly rising consumer demand. before closing i would like to stress that today’s debate will provide an important contribution to the preparation of the cfp reform, but it will also send an important political signal – a positive signal – to the men and women of the european fisheries sector, who are prepared for tougher discipline but are also expecting a message of hope for their future.

in writing. the european parliament refused in february 2010 to sign an eu/us agreement on the transfer of financial data and called for the resumption of negotiations. today the terms of this agreement have been considerably improved in the interests of the european citizen. this time i therefore voted in favour of this agreement, especially since it provides for the establishment of a fully european data mining system in the long term. the agreement is therefore a provisional solution, allowing the european union and the united states to fight terrorism, but it cannot be definitive.
in writing. i have decided to abstain on the eu/us agreement on the transfer of bank data by swift in the context of the fight against terrorism. the agreement is a clear improvement on the previous version. the european parliament, after raising its voice, was able to obtain a number of guarantees that strengthen data protection and the rights of the persons concerned. however, the choice of europol as the authority responsible for the transmission of data is not, in my view, adequate. europol is not an independent authority, but a police agency which i doubt is in a position to exercise neutral control over the compliance of requests for data transmission by the us authorities. because of the highly sensitive nature of the personal data transferred, i could not therefore vote in favour of this agreement.
in writing. i voted for the alvaro report on the new swift agreement which details the conditions for the transfer of certain bank data stored by swift to the us treasury department in the context of the fight against terrorism. using the new powers it has been given since the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon, we have forced the commission to renegotiate a more balanced agreement with the united states. if this agreement is satisfactory, some points could still be improved. today's positive vote is not a blank cheque to the americans: parliament will be able to remain extremely vigilant in the coming months, particularly in the procedure for amending europol's powers, in the appointment of the independent authority present in washington, and in the establishment of a european tftp.
in writing. six months ago, the european parliament stood up for fundamental rights by rejecting the eu-us agreement on the transfer and processing of banking data - the so-called swift agreement. thanks to the efforts of the members of parliament, and in particular of our group, a new model has been developed. it includes substantive improvements such as the elimination of bulk data transfers. the rights of individuals will therefore be better protected while recognising the importance of financial data tracking in the fight against terrorism. that is why i have chosen to vote in favour of the new agreement. but i will continue to pay particular attention to the following: the prerogatives of the european data protection authorities and the choice of europol as the filtering authority; the effectiveness of the 'right to redress' of persons whose privacy rights have been violated; the monitoring and evaluation of the relevance of data transmitted to the us authorities.
in writing. today, after careful consideration, i voted in favour of the revised swift agreement. the compromise is not perfect, but we must combine the demands of the fight against terrorism with respect for civil liberties. secondly, this new version contains improvements, particularly with regard to the purpose of data transmission. as this is a sensitive subject such as the protection of personal data, i would have liked to see more rigour, particularly on the following points: the responsibility for verifying the compliance of requests with the law should be given to an independent authority and not to europol or the right to redress of persons whose rights have been allegedly infringed. in solidarity with my political group, which is responsible for the battle of last february and therefore for most of the progress, i have decided to support this agreement. i will be very attentive, along with my colleagues, to the implementation of the terms of this agreement by the united states, but also very vigilant about the commitments of the council and the commission. if the promises are not kept, i would be in favour of terminating the agreement when the time comes for a review.
in writing. i have followed the negotiations between the eu and the usa on the swift agreement with particular attention since the first rejection, thanks to the action taken by the alde group. and since february, the european parliament, firmly using its new powers, has been able to achieve a great deal of progress and additional guarantees: the 'twin-track' approach advocated by our group, regular reviews of the agreement, a first evaluation in six months, a progress report after three years, a right of access and rectification, the possibility of blocking the transfer of certain data, control by a european authority in the usa of the extraction of data... but while there is much progress, the agreement is not perfect and it also has many weaknesses. it is therefore after careful consideration that i have decided to vote in favour of this new agreement, because a legal framework for the fight against terrorism is necessary, and because we are moving towards a future european system of data transfer control which will allow data to be extracted from european soil. it is now up to the european institutions to monitor closely and vigilantly the implementation of the terms of the agreement.
in writing. i voted for the alvaro report on the eu/us agreement on the transfer and processing of financial messaging data in the context of the fight against terrorism, because i believe that this agreement now strikes a balance between security objectives, in the fight against terrorism, and freedom objectives, in the protection of citizens' privacy. unlike the swift agreement, presented in february, which i voted against, this agreement is more protective of personal data: citizens will have a right of access and rectification to data concerning them, their right to administrative and judicial redress is guaranteed, and several limitations and restrictions have been put on the transfer of data. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environment from harmful substances.

in writing. the convention on cluster munitions aims to prohibit the use, production, stockpiling and transfer of cluster munitions and provides for their removal and destruction. i supported the joint motion for a resolution which calls on all member states to ratify the convention in order to enable the union to accede to it. it is therefore essential to take the necessary steps to ensure that those countries which have not yet ratified the convention do so. for those member states which have already signed the convention, its entry into force is an opportunity to take the necessary measures to implement it, such as destroying stockpiles, removing weapons remnants and providing assistance to victims, etc.
in writing. the lyon report aims to secure and improve the future of the cap after 2013, in line with the context of the economic crisis and the serious financial difficulties faced by member states, taxpayers, farmers and consumers. the european union will thus have to respond to increased demographic pressure and to growing demand from the internal market. but as this report, which i voted for, makes clear, this is not simply an increase in production. the challenge for the cap and for our farmers will be to produce more food with less land, less water and less energy. several amendments were tabled in plenary. i voted in favour of amendment no 1, which stresses the high nutritional value of agricultural products. i voted against amendment no 2, however, which called for the abolition of the two-pillar structure of the cap.
in writing. we are at a pivotal moment in defining what the future reform of the common agricultural policy should be. this is a question that concerns europeans, of course, but also citizens of the world. that is why this reform must not be the business of experts, but of farmers and consumers. the general objectives of a new common agricultural policy must be reconsidered. europeans have new expectations for food. they want an agriculture that respects the environment, that is concerned with quality, traceability, food safety, carbon footprint. this new policy will also have to be part of a global vision. the challenge is to meet the doubling of food needs by 2050 in a context of water scarcity, a decline in arable land and a new energy situation dictated by the fight against climate change. the world organization of agricultural markets must be re-designed in the light of the two main aims of the common agricultural policy: to guarantee food security and to save the livelihood of farmers and their families, both in our own country and in the poorest countries.
in writing. while i welcome this report which is concerned about the future of agriculture, i do not share the view that the cap has succeeded in achieving the objectives of ensuring a fair standard of living, stabilising markets, producing quality food at reasonable prices, developing rural activity, guaranteeing our health security and food sovereignty. the reality is different. just look at the state of a large agricultural nation like france, which shows in its accounts a 34% decline in income. as in the past, the cap after 2013 will not be able to protect our farmers from speculators and unbridled global competition, nor will it be able to counter the deviousness of the multinational agro-food industries and the retail sector. the post-2013 cap will remain stuck between the ultra-liberal and globalist market logic of the european commission and a future "green" cap, which is actually serving the neo-capitalists of eco-business. this is a logic which sacrifices our rural environment, not for the benefit of poor countries or the disadvantaged or desertified regions of europe, and which justifies the urgent need to renationalize the cap.
in writing. i voted in favour of the lyon report on the future of the cap, and in particular for the maintenance of the two pillars. the vote on the lyon report in plenary today is very important and symbolic, since the elected members of the european parliament are the first to take a stand and present their proposal for the cap after 2013. i have every confidence in commissioner cioloş that he will take the results of this vote into account in the proposals that will be put forward in november by the european commission. the main priorities of european agriculture, such as food security, market regulation and spatial planning, are clearly reaffirmed, as are the budgetary implications, which must be in line with the ambitions of the cap. measures to support biodiversity should not be forgotten. biodiversity must be at the heart of the cap's system, because its protection is no longer a luxury for the conservation of species and environments.
in writing. the text has the merit of acknowledging market failures and advocating for the fight against climate change. that's as far as his merit goes. despite the acknowledged shortcomings, the text promotes market liberalisation, farmers' responsiveness to market signals, the competitiveness of european agriculture on global and regional markets, and green capitalism. this framework is in no way a means of combating global warming, nor is it the carbon market, agrofuels and gmos that this text is taking advantage of. instead, it's promoting productivism and the devastation of local food farms here and around the world.
in writing. this own-initiative report, which deals with the import regime for fishery and aquaculture products (faps) into the eu, aims to advocate the maintenance of environmentally friendly and economically viable fisheries and aquaculture sectors in the eu in the long term. we are seeing an increase in imports of fishery and aquaculture products at the expense of our community production. i agree with the rapporteur that it is essential to restore our community production. however, we are aware, as our rapporteur in the lead, that this must be done in a manner consistent with sustainable management; for example, the amount of fish caught must be limited in order to manage our natural resources. in addition, it seems necessary to promote responsible consumption in which quality and sustainability of production are paramount.
in writing. like agriculture, fisheries and aquaculture are not suited to a purely free trade approach. eu production is unable to meet european demand, which is already 60% covered by imported products. but we must ensure that the future import regimes in the eu strike the right balance so that european production, which is already in crisis, does not suffer from unfair competition with third countries. in the world trade organisation (wto) negotiations, fishery products should be considered as 'sensitive products' on the same basis as certain agricultural products, which would facilitate the maintenance of customs duties on imports from third countries. european fishermen would thus be protected by a reasonable and flexible customs duty and an eco-label. at the same time, developing countries must be able to develop their own fisheries. to this end, we must ask ourselves whether international agreements allowing the purchase of fishing rights from developing countries, allowing fleets from third countries to fish industrially along their coasts, depriving them of a huge part of their natural resources, are appropriate.

the rapporteur. - madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would first of all like to thank all my colleagues on the committee on agriculture, and in particular the fictitious rapporteurs, for their support in this work. this report is part of our great debate on the reform of the cap, like mr lyon's report. we have managed to agree on a large number of compromises, which were adopted by a large majority in our group, 32 votes to 4. i think our message to the commission is clear: we all want more transparency in the food chain and legislation that guarantees fair competition between farmers and all the actors in the food chain. we also want concrete action in europe and elsewhere to combat speculation and abuse of market power and to provide income for farmers. i am surprised that, at the initiative of a few political groups in this parliament, we are being asked to vote tomorrow on a long list of separate votes which run counter to the strong and consensual message which we adopted by a large majority in committee. is it possible that the summer has changed your mind? i have the impression that the intensive lobbying of the retail trade and certain players in the agri-food industry in recent days is the cause of the plethora of separate votes. in any case, i cannot imagine, ladies and gentlemen, that you would give in to these pressures to weaken our common message. our committee has taken stock of the crisis affecting european farmers. it intends to propose concrete and strong measures: in less than ten years, the union has lost three and a half million agricultural jobs. the carnage is dramatic. bulgaria, for example, lost one farmer in two. in 2009, the revenue collapsed. in france and germany, farmers lost an average of 20% of their income, in hungary more than 35%. agriculture and the rural world are threatened with extinction. in december 2009, driven by the anger of farmers and the protests of dairy farmers, the european commission published a communication entitled 'a more efficient food supply chain in europe'. it shows that between 1995 and 2005 the share of value added in the food chain going to agricultural producers increased from 31% to 24%. prices paid to farmers are falling in virtually all sectors without benefiting european consumers. the commission states that these problems are linked to the increase in concentration at the level of wholesalers, processors and distributors, who impose their will on producers who are not very well organized. the commission is concerned about the lack of transparency in the formation of prices and margins. it recognises the difficulty of obtaining accurate and reliable data and admits that it does not have the information necessary to adapt its policies quickly and effectively. to remedy this, i propose that the commission set up a european observatory of agricultural prices and margins, similar to the one in the united states. this body will be responsible for determining the production costs of european farmers. it will enable us to know the real costs, when we leave the farm, of a litre of milk, a kilo of wheat or a kilo of beef. these indications will serve as a basis for negotiation between farmers and other actors in the food chain. the agency will also be responsible for assessing the sectors which capture the most value added at the expense of producers and consumers. the european commission would then be able to identify those actors who are abusing the balance of power and who are abusing a dominant position. it is also essential to get the 20 largest european companies to report annually on their market shares and internal margins. transparency is not a danger to the market economy. on the contrary, it is absolutely necessary to avoid the deviations which have been observed in agriculture and in many other sectors, especially in the financial sector. when the farmer sells his milk or his meat, who can claim to be on an equal footing with a multinational company that weighs on the formation of commodity prices at the level of world markets? the balance of power is totally unbalanced, some would say unfair. to put things right, a first emergency measure would be to allow farmers to form producer organizations. the second, complementary, is the prohibition at union level of the sale of goods below cost. forced discounts, ex post modifications of contractual terms, unjustified referencing fees are commonplace. they are a blow to farmers and the thousands of small and medium-sized processing companies, which have to go through the large distribution system to market their products. the european commission must identify the extent of these anti-economic practices and take the necessary measures to put an end to them. finally, speculation on agricultural products is a scourge. the investors and speculators are looking for a price and immediate profits. poverty, hunger and starvation are synonymous with profit. we thought we wouldn't have the riots of 2008. but it is not. since june, the price of wheat has risen by more than 70%. the corn, soybean and rice farmers are doing the same. last week in maputo, mozambique, seven people were killed because they were protesting against a 30% increase in food prices. are we going to sit around and do nothing, like two years ago? we are not going to tolerate investment banks bankrupting european farmers and destroying the people of our planet. i call on the european union to take the initiative in creating a global market regulation agency. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would ask you to send a strong signal that the new cap is fairer for european farmers and consumers, that fair competition is established between the players, that it creates a regulatory framework for the markets and that it excludes speculators. it is the responsibility of the european parliament, on the eve of the exercise of its co-decision in agricultural matters, not to give in to any pressure, wherever it may come from. our message must remain clear and consistent.
for the gue/ngl group madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the majority of farmers in the union survive on a meagre income and are, moreover, constantly subject to the stress of irrational speculation on the financial markets. most farmers are convinced that they have no future. they are one of the most affected by suicide. if europe continues to impoverish its farmers and agricultural workers, this will lead to their disappearance, with terrible consequences for land use, quality of life and food independence. this will fuel an ecological crisis with effects even more dire and faster than the melting of the greenland ice sheet. the text is full of good resolutions and interesting proposals, although it is not very clear what the root causes of the current disaster are and therefore there are radical solutions to be found. the problem is not only to ensure that farmers and agricultural workers, who are largely forgotten in this resolution, receive a fair income, but also to achieve a level of income and a price that will enable the whole agricultural world to live off its labour. we must point the finger and punish, if necessary, the large retailers and the financial funds behind them, for their reckless pressure to lower prices, but also for the slow settlement of debts, the funds that speculate on food production, exposing our people to great risks, and the role of the banks in the difficulties of the peasants. it is a report that is moving in the right direction, but it is not the only one.

mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i am a philosophically liberal. in economics, i believe in the virtue of the market and competition. but to those in this house who think that agriculture can be treated by the same usual market rules, i say this: do you know of any other sector as important as agriculture in the economy that has such unpredictability and such possible variation in its prices? some european farmers, it has been said, have seen their incomes fall by 50 per cent. who here would want to see their income split in half? who can say that this is a dignified and fair situation? besides, these prices are crazy, they're for everyone. they prevent farmers from benefiting from increases and they prevent consumers from benefiting from decreases. so yes, the real question is price legibility; it is the value added of work. in my mind, mr president, agriculture is not a nostalgia for a bygone era. agriculture is the guarantee of the future. it is the guarantee for europe of a regular and guaranteed supply of its 500 million inhabitants. now, who here knows of a single great country in history that has not been concerned about its food supply? we must do for agriculture what has been done for the financial sector. i am not saying that the commission should not be involved in this. europe, my dear colleagues, needs its farmers. and i want to tell mr bové that he has my vote and, i am sure, the vote of many epp members.
mr commissioner, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to congratulate the work of the committee on agriculture and, therefore, mr bové. the volatility of food and raw material prices creates great difficulties for our farmers. their average income fell by more than 12% in the european union in 2009, with peaks of minus 50% for some incomes. our farmers must be able to earn a living from their work on the one hand and to produce food that meets high quality standards at an affordable price for the consumer on the other. our three challenges are therefore: to guarantee farmers profitable volumes and prices so that they can produce in a stable, safe and, above all, profitable way, with a view to their future income; to improve the balance of the food chain and price transparency in the interest of the consumer; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the policy benefits farmers and consumers and not other links which are currently complicating the sector. the report by mr bové, thanks to the work done in the committee on agriculture, is balanced. it offers some solutions to the challenges i have just identified. in my view, new market regulation is needed, based in particular on better integration of the various links in the chain. strengthening producer organisations, proposing standard contracts in certain sectors, encouraging self-regulation initiatives, these are good ways of working in my view. it is also essential to promote quality products and sustainable production, and for this we need a credible european system, quality labels and signs. the agricultural market needs regulation, but it needs proportionate and intelligent regulation.
