in writing. following the 2002 floods which caused great damage to people and property in germany, austria, the czech republic and france, the council of the european union created an instrument to provide rapid funding for the relief of regions affected by natural disasters. today, ireland, which has itself been hit by floods, is to benefit from this fund. i voted in favour of this amendment to the eu budget because it allows this aid to be paid to our irish friends. this vote is a symbol of european solidarity in the face of natural disasters. this is expressed today in ireland and tomorrow in france. indeed, our country will soon receive substantial financial assistance to deal with the aftermath of the storm xynthia in february 2010.
in writing. in the region, moldova has one of the lowest human development index. the policies of forced liberalization for the benefit of the financial elites of the european union are largely responsible for this. the european commission and the imf, which have promised to provide macrofinancial assistance, will only make the situation worse. in these circumstances, it is cynical to accept that the moldovan government is forcing its people to finance european programmes and agencies as questionable as the competitiveness and innovation framework programme or the sesar programme, even though moldova is not a member of the european union. i am voting against this report.
in writing. parliament adopted two legislative reports on first reading on wednesday: a regulation on aspects specific to the european union and a directive on the rules to be applied by the member states at national level. member states will be responsible for national regulation to ensure that objective and impartial information is available to the general public. this includes package leaflets, a product assessment report and information on how to prevent disease. patients should have better access to quality information on prescription medicines. this involves information about the characteristics of a medicine and the diseases it treats. we must protect consumers and keep them informed in a transparent way. a europe that protects and informs is also our job as a european parliamentarian, and that is why i voted in favour of these two texts.
in writing. directive 2001/83/ec establishes a community code relating to medicinal products for human use. it lays down rules on the information to be attached to medicinal products on their characteristics and use. however, it does not provide a harmonised framework on the content and quality of non-advertising information for patients. experience has also shown that unequal interpretation of texts can lead to situations where the public is exposed to disguised advertising, particularly on the internet. the commission has proposed a directive amending the existing regulation to improve the dissemination of information to the public on prescription medicines. it aims to establish a legal framework governing the provision of specific information on medicinal products by marketing authorisation holders to the public. the european parliament has prepared a more ambitious legislative resolution than the commission 's proposal . i voted for this text because it improves and secures the information given to patients a little more.
in writing. in healthcare, access to comprehensive and quality information is a guarantee of better outcomes, as patients are more likely to follow treatment they can understand. i agree with the rapporteur that it is difficult to access such information in some european countries, because of the different interpretations of the directive on medicinal products by the member states, and because of the lack of reliability and clarity of the data. it is necessary to ensure better access to this information, in accordance with the patient's right to information. however, in order not to create any imbalance between member states, it is essential to identify the medium for disseminating this information, without favouring one over the other. finally, it is essential to distinguish clearly between information and advertising and to prevent pharmaceutical companies from taking advantage of these information campaigns to promote their products.
in writing. i voted against this because we cannot allow the pharmaceutical companies and the commission to make health a commodity like any other. the link between the pharmaceutical industry in europe and pharmacovigilance is once again at the heart of the debate. the pharmaceutical companies cannot be allowed to inform the public freely and to advertise prescription drugs directly to the general public. their commercial concerns are incompatible with the public interest objectives of our health policies and it would be dangerous to allow them to do so.
in writing. a distinction between information and advertising about medicines is essential for the protection of citizens. that is why i voted in favour of the report by christofer fjellner, which requires an objective description of the patient's address on the packaging of medicinal products. in addition, access to clear and reliable information will be enhanced by making it available in all eu languages, on labelled websites or in official brochures. i welcome the adoption of this proposal, which is a real step towards greater transparency in health.
in writing. the amendments which this house is making to the commission and council proposal are not all in the right direction. they never deviate from the logic of the single market in medicines and continue to regard those of them which are not subject to prescription as goods like any other; the authors end up talking about "consumers" instead of patients. they do not propose to prevent pharmaceutical companies from producing information on their medicines for the general public. however, they have the merit of seeking to enable states to regulate as much as possible the disclosure of information published by these firms. in particular, they give them the right to publicly denounce those who publish information that does not conform to official state data or who disseminate it in a misleading way. it's better than nothing. i cannot, however, vote for such a weak text. i'll abstain from it.
in writing. regulation (ec) no 726/2004 establishes community procedures for the authorisation and supervision of medicinal products for human and veterinary use and establishes a european medicines agency. the amendment to directive 2001/83/ec has focused on better information for patients, particularly as regards the distinction with advertising. following that amendment, the regulation should be amended to also subject a number of information relating to the products to which it relates to prior control by the european medicines agency. with this in mind, the european commission has drawn up a proposal to amend the regulation as regards the dissemination to the public of information on medicinal products for human use subject to medical prescription. the european parliament, which was called upon to give its opinion on the proposal, made a number of amendments to the commission's text. these are the same reasons which led me to vote in favour of the resolution amending directive 2001/83/ec. the two pieces of legislation go hand in hand to improve information for patients about the medicines they are given.
in writing. this report is a reminder of what the european medicines agency should be. we cannot object to a draft which states the obvious, such as the need to 'emphasise the rights and interests of patients', the need to oblige companies to publicly list the side effects of their medicines or the need to publish information in all the official languages of the european union. it is also a matter of concern that such common places should be reopened 15 years after the establishment of the agency! parliament should denounce the opacity of this agency and declare loudly that it must be reformed in the interests of all.
in writing. every year, about 9.3 million tonnes of electronic waste are produced in europe. however, these equipment often contain a significant amount of highly polluting products. this waste is a major environmental challenge. in addition to reprocessing, it is essential to limit the use of these dangerous substances from the outset. the major industrial groups have already begun to limit this use. however, clear rules are needed to provide a common framework for this vital effort. i therefore voted in favour of the european parliament's legislative resolution to adopt a directive restricting the use of these substances. this vote was not easy, however. the proposal contains a number of exemptions, particularly as regards solar panels. as they reduce greenhouse gas emissions, we thought it would be appropriate to tolerate the substances they contain. this has, however, naturally been the subject of debate on the priorities of the union's environmental policy. the latter unfortunately faces conflicting issues.
in writing. in co-decision, the european parliament endorsed the agreement with the council by adopting at first reading the recast of the directive on the restriction of the use of certain hazardous substances in electrical and electronic equipment. this is good news for european consumers: electrical and electronic equipment sold in the european union accounts for a significant share of consumer goods sold (an estimated 9.3 million tonnes of electrical and electronic equipment are sold each year in the european union alone). the increasingly frequent replacement of these various equipment raises the question of the waste and hazardous substances contained in this waste. it is necessary, for reasons of public safety and health, to limit their use. the idea, with this revision of the current directive dating from 2003, is to make even more progress in limiting the use of dangerous substances. it is also planned that the commission will review its legislation in three years' time, in order to adapt the legislation to future innovations.
in writing. waste electrical and electronic equipment is increasing and includes several hazardous substances. these substances can be released into the environment and harm human health if not handled appropriately. this directive will enable many companies to make even greater progress in designing new and safer electrical and electronic equipment by encouraging technological innovation. the reduction of hazardous substances upstream will also lead to lower recycling costs. finally, and this is a crucial point, we have obtained the exclusion of photovoltaic panels in order to encourage the development of renewable energy technologies in europe.
in writing. the resolution on the acta (international agreement on counterfeiting and counterfeiting of financial instruments) was voted in parliament today, with a view to better enforcing anti-counterfeiting measures at international level. the ccca is a tool to make existing rules more effective and to provide better protection against infringement of copyright, trademarks, patents, designs and geographical indications. i voted in favour of this resolution, tabled by my group, the epp, because i believe that the acca is a shield for european industry. this will enable us to ensure the protection of copyright, as well as creativity and innovation in cultural and scientific fields. today we must stop and think about how to fight piracy more effectively, and this international agreement is a step towards better enforcement of anti-counterfeiting measures.
in writing. i voted in favour of the joint resolution proposed by the epp and the ecr on the anti-counterfeiting trade agreement, known as acta. the aim of the agreement is to combat the proliferation of counterfeits and the increase in piracy of copyrighted products by establishing a new international governance structure. it is essential to protect creation against theft through piracy and counterfeiting. the union, which aims to become the most competitive knowledge-based economy in the world, cannot remain indifferent to this major problem. that is why i welcome the adoption of this resolution. this is a strong text which should have brought all members of the european parliament together. unfortunately, it was adopted by a very small majority. while the european commission offered strong guarantees on respect for fundamental freedoms, the left in the european parliament preferred to lock themselves in protest slogans without any foundation. in my view, the european union must be at the forefront of this fight against the negligence and ill-will often shown by china and russia in this area. it is about our competitiveness in the global economy.
in writing. i voted against this text: the european right has given in to the demands of certain governments and the pressure of the cultural industries, to the detriment of the fundamental freedoms of european citizens. all the safeguards we asked the commission to take were swept away in one fell swoop by the european people's party. this is a bad signal to the commission in the run-up to the sydney negotiations next week. in addition, the vague definition of the term 'commercial scale' associated with the increase in criminal sanctions for online copyright infringement could encourage states to adopt legislation leading to the criminalisation of private users and technical intermediaries. acta must not lead to the european union being able to conduct its own investigations and to introduce graduated or equivalent response systems! finally, the commission should conduct an impact assessment rapidly before acta is implemented and not after on its implementation and its implications for fundamental rights, data protection and the e-commerce directive.
in writing. there is still doubt about the content of the acta agreement! the main purpose of this agreement, which was negotiated in the utmost secrecy for years by about ten countries, is to combat counterfeiting and protect intellectual property rights. however, it should be noted that neither china, brazil nor india participated in these negotiations. moreover, if counterfeiting is to be tackled, the known provisions of the treaty in question imply the introduction of measures that can be considered as infringements of individual freedoms: surveillance of internet service providers, strengthening of border controls, and more difficult transit of low-cost generic medicines for developing countries. these concerns were echoed by many members of parliament, who did not want to place their 'blind' trust in the negotiations conducted by the european commission. the resolution adopted by a narrow majority cannot be considered as support, as doubts remain as to whether the text is in conformity with the acquis communautaire and whether it is compatible with respect for fundamental rights.
in writing. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, if i had not decided to boycott the sitting after the regrettable episode of social-eurocratic totalitarianism that we have just experienced, i would have voted in favour of the joint resolution of the left-wing groups on the agreement on counterfeiting. not because i have changed my political views, but because i believe that this agreement is not sufficient to protect our industries from counterfeiting, that it does not guarantee respect for geographical indications, that it is of little use if it does not concern china, the world's largest counterfeiter, and that it endangers the rights and freedoms of citizens in relation to "intangible" property rights. i also support all the requests for prior information, impact studies, etc. made in this resolution. in short, the agreement as it stands is useless and potentially harmful. it should not even be under negotiation, let alone, given the issues it covers, by the european commission alone.
in writing. i voted against the resolution on the anti-counterfeiting trade agreement tabled by the epp and the ecr because this text is totally insufficient in protecting individual freedoms. meps have repeatedly expressed their many concerns when, during the negotiation of this international agreement and before the final signature of the agreement by the states and the european union, it was important to raise a number of issues, including access to medicines, the responsibility of internet service providers, or the search of travellers' personal luggage at borders. unfortunately, the joint resolution tabled by the s&d, greens/efa, alde and gue/ngl groups, which i voted for, expressing these concerns, was not adopted by a few votes.
in writing. i voted in favour of the epp-ecr resolution on the anti-counterfeiting trade agreement. the resolution recalls that the fight against counterfeiting is a priority in the eu's internal and international political strategy and that international cooperation is a key element in pursuing this objective at global level. taking up the concerns of the european parliament and our fellow citizens such as respect for fundamental rights, the protection of privacy and personal data, the recognition of the essential role of free internet, the importance of protecting the role of service providers and the need to safeguard access to medicines, the act makes existing rules more effective. it aims to ensure better protection against all infringements of intellectual property rights, trademarks, designs, designs and patents in the interests of community exports and right holders. contrary to what has been said by its critics, the agreement is fully compatible with the acquis communautaire. it does not, for example, introduce the so-called 'three-stage graduated response' procedure.
in writing. the anti-counterfeiting trade agreement (acta) was negotiated behind the backs of citizens and against the un and its world intellectual property organization, the only legitimate entity to implement this type of agreement. a handful of countries have negotiated with the acca the rules that will prevail in the field of intellectual property rights. this confiscation of international law for the benefit of the richest countries and their closest allies is intolerable. so when there is a growing doubt about the patentability of living organisms or about possible obstacles to the marketing of generic medicines, the urgency is not to lament or regret this by accepting the fact of the matter. i am voting against this text.
in writing. i am in favour of the anti-counterfeiting trade agreement (acta) because it is an agreement that protects our citizens, our creators, our artists and our businesses. it clarifies the remedies available in the event of a flagrant infringement of intellectual property rights in one of the countries party to the agreement. the commission has been transparent, acac cannot go beyond the acquis communautaire, cannot go beyond the measures taken within the framework of european directives, cannot in any case violate fundamental rights. it was negotiated outside the traditional international bodies (wto...) because china and india refused any agreement! finally, the acac is open, and all the states that freely wish to participate can join us, so that together we can protect our citizens, legally as well as physically, from the damage of counterfeiting. i therefore voted in favour of this resolution.
in writing. i voted in favour of my group's resolution because the fight against counterfeiting is essential and must be global if it is to be effective. counterfeiting is a growing parallel economy and allows the massive laundering of dirty money. moreover, our industries, already suffering from the export penalty of the undervalued yuan and the weak dollar, cannot tolerate the unfair competition of counterfeits produced outside the eu with their products on the domestic market. this globally organized theft is taking a heavy toll on creativity and innovation and has disastrous consequences for our jobs and the safety of deceived consumers. our development model, which is geared towards a knowledge-based economy, requires the protection of this fundamental right of intellectual property on a global scale. the vote now opens the way for the ratification of the anti-counterfeiting trade agreement, which will facilitate the possibility of legal remedies in the event of infringement of intellectual property rights in the signatory states. we are thus laying the foundations for a multilateral strategy that will protect the driving force of our economic development: our inventions, our brands and our artistic works.
for the greens/efa group mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i could have limited my speech to simply recalling the images of this summer in russia or south asia, recalling the absolute urgency of combating climate change, and since we are talking about europe, to move immediately or as soon as possible to a 30% target by 2020 in terms of reducing greenhouse gas emissions. today, if we don't change anything, we'll be at 19%. we are already very close to the target we set ourselves, so we can no longer speak of european ambition when we talk about 20 per cent. i am not necessarily a believer in the carbon market, but if we stay at 20%, the fact is that we will treat the carbon market as an endangered species and not as a lever to fight climate change. if we go up to 30%, this could potentially be €8 billion, including auctions of allowances, in the eu budgets. 30% is a possibility. if we set a binding target of 20% energy efficiency, this would mean a million jobs in europe. that is a saving of €1,000 per european household, and since commissioner oettinger was talking about nabucco, 20% energy savings in europe is the equivalent of 15 nabucco. so are we going to kill european companies if we go to 30%? of course not. i'm not going to. all the studies show it. a few potentially risky sectors are affected, but the tools are there and so far the sectors that threaten europe with annihilation are the sectors that have gained in european energy policy. they have made billions of euros from european climate policy. to go to 30 percent is to be clearly on the side of those who make the change, is to be on the side of those who make the world of tomorrow. and i would like to quote a few figures. according to ernst young's 2010 barometer, china and the united states are the most attractive countries for renewable energy development. according to a recent study, of the 50 companies identified as the world's green technology leaders, only three are in europe, the others are in asia or the united states. so we absolutely need to get to 30%, and i'll end with a quote from barack obama: "we can either abandon the jobs of the future to our competitors, or we can, as they have already begun to do, seize the opportunity of the century. the nation that pioneers the energies of the future will be the nation that pioneers the 21st century". he lost the election. take this leadership in energy transition and new economy.
mr president, madam minister, madam commissioner, since copenhagen, at least one thing is certain, that the disinformation operation which was set up before copenhagen has failed and that the information given to us by the ipcc has been perfectly confirmed by all the expertise carried out by the un. that is the first point i wanted to make. this shows the importance and urgency of our action. we have to learn from the failure in copenhagen and it is therefore absolutely essential that the european union sets itself extremely ambitious targets, and that is why it is essential, both for the climate and for our industry and our economy, that the 30% target in the resolution can be voted on tomorrow. as one of our colleagues has just pointed out, the 20% target is already almost achieved. if we want to boost our industry, if we want to remain leaders or become leaders in new sectors, whether energy efficiency or renewable energy, it is essential to have this objective in the union. the second point is credibility. we must keep our commitments to the countries of the south, distinguishing between the different categories of countries of the south, because china and africa cannot really be put in the same category. that is why, in my view - and this is my personal opinion, not necessarily that of my whole group - it is essential to have a financial transaction tax which will help us to reach the $100 billion we have planned for 2020. finally, i hope at least that the agreement on forests, the redd agreement, can be concluded in cancún, because that would be a great step forward. let's remember that deforestation is responsible for 20 percent of greenhouse gas emissions.
mr president, commissioner, minister, i hope that unity and realism will be lost tomorrow when we vote on our resolution on the 16th conference of the parties on climate change. i hope that our commissioner will be able to take up the pragmatic objectives that we must achieve collectively, but also defend the sine qua non conditions that europe has set. in these negotiations we must not lose sight of the legitimate expectations of our citizens and our industries for fairness. it is the world that must fight climate change, not europe alone. thus, recognising the importance of intellectual property that is not sufficiently protected will be essential. green technologies must benefit the greatest number of people, but we must not sell our present and future knowledge, even in the fight against climate change. similarly, the demand for common methods of calculating emissions and for the verification and publication of data so that all emitters are subject to the same scale seems to be a legitimate demand and not a negotiating tool. finally, more controversially - and my colleague raised this earlier - the shortcomings of the current system of own development mechanisms will also be brought to the table. we are all aware, ladies and gentlemen, that the real power of negotiation does not lie with the european parliament. but the will of many members of the european parliament, including myself, to work and to contribute to a positive outcome of this conference must be encouraged and not neglected as we have seen in recent days. if europe wants to be strong in international dialogues, it must be strong for all its legislators.
mr president, commissioner, we know your pugnacity and your desire that europe finally speak with one voice in cancún. so i would like to ask you to give us your views on two subjects, two actions which are in our resolution which will be put to the vote tomorrow. i would like to know your public opinion on these two proposals before the vote tomorrow. first, the creation of a green fund, which will finally provide, from 2020, 100 billion dollars a year to help the poorest countries. secondly, the introduction of a 0.01% tax on financial transactions, which will provide a financial source of eur 20 billion to help the poorest countries. i think this is an important subject in financial matters to enable us to move faster and further.

the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the subject of this report is being debated in the international community. developing countries believe that developed countries use human rights clauses to introduce a form of disguised protectionism, while developed countries denounce social and environmental dumping by emerging countries. i wanted to take a positive approach by showing how social and environmental standards and commercial interests can be mutually reinforcing if all countries play by the same rules. the european union must play its part in international trade to bring about change. it would act in accordance with its founding texts, which state that the european union must contribute to sustainable development, free and fair trade and the protection of human rights. i believe that its action must be undertaken simultaneously at multilateral, bilateral and unilateral levels. at the multilateral level, the european union should encourage international organisations, in particular the world trade organisation, to take greater account of social and environmental standards. these international organisations must also strengthen their cooperation. that is why i am proposing, in particular, that the international labour organisation be granted observer status in the wto. on the environment, i believe that access to green goods and technologies should be a priority because they not only promote new forms of employment policy but also create new growth opportunities for european companies that are very successful in this field. the establishment of a genuine world environmental organization which could be seized in the event of environmental dumping should also be considered. the european union can really set an example at the bilateral level. while i welcome the fact that the new generation of free trade agreements contain a binding human rights clause, i would like to see this practice extended to the sustainable development chapter as well. in addition, the european commission negotiates such agreements. it should include a set of social and environmental standards to be respected by all its trading partners. these basic standards could be supplemented on a case-by-case basis by additional conventions depending on the degree of economic, social and environmental development of the country concerned. this gradual and flexible treatment would make it possible to deal more fairly with our various trading partners and would be more equitable for all. in particular, the monitoring of the implementation of bilateral agreements must be strengthened. i therefore propose that impact assessments be carried out before, during and after the negotiations and that they no longer only cover sustainable development but also human rights. finally, i am hopeful that things will move quickly unilaterally, since the system of generalised preferences should be reformed very soon. as you know, the gsp requires ratification of some 30 international conventions on human rights, the environment, labour and good governance. the european union has a duty to ensure that the european union is able to take action in the fight against terrorism. the commission must launch investigations or even withdraw preferences if there are indications that the conventions are not being applied. in conclusion, some of these actions can be taken now but attitudes will not change overnight. the european union must act gradually and at all levels to achieve a fairer balance in trade relations.
the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i believe that at the very moment when the european union is trying to redefine its trade policy after the treaty of lisbon, and at the same time trying to link it with its industrial policy, it is welcome that three reports are being presented to this parliament at the same time on issues which ultimately fall within the same field of political debate and public debate on 'what is trade and how is trade linked to social issues, environmental issues or human rights issues'? in fact, we are in a permanent state of schizophrenia: companies are moving to other countries, social rights are being called into question, environmental damage is increasing, and at the same time we are negotiating free trade agreements, we are negotiating a whole series of measures within the wto which, unfortunately, are completely out of step with the public debate in which citizens are trying to engage. how can we explain to our public opinion today that a football which is sold on the european market, produced under decent working conditions which respect the environment, and a football which is made by child labour or in a country where trade union organisation is prohibited, are the same football? we can no longer explain this to our public opinions; so we have to - it's our responsibility today - integrate these environmental and social issues into trade. on my report specifically, in relation to trade, there are a number of countries in europe today whose imports of products are very much offsetting the declines in their own emissions. a third of europe's emissions are not produced in europe but are imported goods. it is therefore essential that we integrate climate change into our trade. how can we explain to our public opinion that at the same time as we are going to conclude a free trade agreement which will potentially lead to deforestation, we are going to negotiate in cancún a redd agreement which aims to compensate financially, in the countries of the south, for non-deforestation? it is therefore essential to be able to make the connection between these different subjects. when we made this report - and i would like to thank the fictitious rapporteurs from the various groups - we tried to be as constructive as possible. i hope that will be reflected in the vote tomorrow. we tried to end the debate on black and white. we have stopped saying that trade liberalization and the fight against climate change will destroy 100 per cent of our industries in europe, where, in a way, we don't care because the climate issue must come first. when we worked on the issue of carbon leakage, for example, we tried to specify in each case which sector of activity could be put at risk and what tools could be used to protect this sector. the same is true of the wto framework laws, the anti-dumping laws. the same applies to production processes and methods. on all these subjects, we have tried, with the other groups, to have proposals which will make it possible to move things forward and which are, i believe, concrete in relation to our ambitions, in relation to the mandate of the european commission and of all the european institutions. i would simply say that, once again, i hope that tomorrow the cooperative, constructive spirit in which we have drawn up this report will be reflected in the vote and, once again, i would like to thank all my colleagues for the work they have done.
the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i too would like to begin by thanking my colleagues in the committee on international trade and, in particular, the fictitious rapporteurs of the various groups for their cooperation in the preparation of this third report on a related subject, which allows us to present today a set of innovative and concrete proposals to advance corporate social responsibility within the framework of the european union's trade policy. after the international crisis, the economic and social damage it has caused, but also the debates it has provoked, the expectations of citizens and the political expectations that have been expressed to learn from it, our common conviction is that europe's trade policy must more than ever contribute to the objectives of regulating globalisation, and in particular to its social and environmental objectives. this regulation concerns states and their economies, but of course the main economic actors are companies and, in particular, multinational companies, which are the main actors in world trade. they have benefited more than anyone else from the opening of markets, not only to access consumers but also to outsource part of their production and diversify their supply chain, often from countries with low production costs and, above all, with less stringent social and environmental rules. trade liberalization has been accompanied by fierce competition between countries to attract foreign investment and increased competition between firms, and this has too often led to intolerable abuses of working conditions, violations of human rights and damage to the environment. from the bhopal disaster in the indian subsidiary of a multinational chemical company, which left thousands of victims, to the impunity of the parent company today, to the behaviour of oil and mining companies in africa, burma and many other countries, which are destroying their environment, reducing their workers to slavery, from child labour in textile factories in asia to the murders of trade unionists on farms in central america, there are many examples. and they are all the more unacceptable because they often concern companies from industrialized countries, their subsidiaries, their supply chains, including european companies. this has given rise, for many years now, to a debate and a struggle, which has been repeatedly echoed in this parliament by the adoption of resolutions on the social and environmental responsibility of enterprises. so far, progress in csr has not been met by the debate on social standards in trade agreements, the subject of mrs saïfi's report. this is both understandable, because trade agreements are about binding legal rules between states, while corporate social responsibility is about voluntary commitments by companies, but at the same time it is paradoxical, because csr and social and environmental clauses are pushing in the same direction, that is, towards a globalisation that is more in line with human rights, the environment and sustainable development. we therefore propose to introduce csr in trade agreements and, in concrete terms, to introduce a corporate social responsibility clause in the sustainable development chapters, in particular of ftas, with a number of clear and verifiable commitments by companies. first, there must be a reciprocal commitment by the european union and its partners to encourage companies to make commitments and to verify them: opening of contact points, so that information can be available, but also so that testimonies, in particular from trade unionists and civil society, can be given; the commission has also adopted a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work. finally, we propose that in the event of failure, serious breaches of csr commitments, but also breaches of social rights, social and environmental laws, there should be mechanisms to ... mr president, ladies and gentlemen, by defending free trade and organising the union's commercial disarmament, the commission has played its full role as a servile instrument serving very particular interests, which are harmful to european workers. free and undistorted competition is a myth that destroys jobs and lives. if competition is free, then all dumping is possible, starting with tax, social, monetary and environmental dumping, and competition is distorted. to get out of this situation which is killing industrial employment and plunging workers and their families into poverty, it is necessary to establish strict controls on capital movements by the member states, to destroy tax havens, to take the essential sectors for life - energy, water, medicines, agriculture and training - out of the market and, above all, to define and enforce environmental and social criteria which guarantee equality in commercial activity and the rights of workers.
member of the commission. − mr president, i think this has been a very rich debate. while the philosophy behind the three reports is similar, the details, ideas and responses we have shared today cannot be addressed adequately in the short time at my disposal. some ideas are workable, others less so, because we operate in a legal, an institutional and a political framework, both as a union of 27 member states and as a member of the wto. i will try to highlight what i believe to be the salient considerations for each report. unfortunately i cannot be exhaustive. on the saïfi report, a number of you have raised the possibility of ilo observer status in the wto. my starting point is that there is definitely much scope for improved international governance and better coordination between international organisations. my next consideration is that, in order to leverage trade policy to achieve a better social and environmental outcome, we need to set feasible objectives. structural changes take a long time to implement and, if we are realistic about the wto membership coming round to a ‘trade and...’ agenda, this is a long-term endeavour. let me add that, with regard to the proposal in the saïfi report that there should be a human rights assessment of free trade agreements (ftas), i believe this should happen throughout the negotiations. i would be rather sceptical about having a special period between the end of the negotiations and the initialling of the agreement. this was also discussed this morning in another context, but i think we should stick to the procedure in the lisbon treaty which makes it very clear that it is up to the commission to initial such agreements; after that, the ratification procedure starts and the council signs, which is their way of ratifying; then the european parliament has the right and the duty to ratify by vote. with regard to the idea of having a human rights assessment before the initialling – let us call it a kind of pre-condition – i would not be positive about this. on the other hand, i think the actual idea of assessing the human rights impact of an agreement makes sense, and i am positive on that. specific questions have also been put, for example on child labour. you know that we are currently negotiating a free trade agreement with india, where the whole matter of sustainability also has to be addressed. india is very sceptical about such a sustainability chapter in the agreement, but we insist – and we will continue to insist – that such a chapter has its place, and i think that ultimately it will be included. i would simply like to ask that, later on when you will have to discuss this, you take into account the fact that the ideas of individual third countries on such a sustainability chapter may concern not only the content of it but also the philosophy of certain third countries on this issue. with respect to the jadot report, i have heard calls for a climate chapter in each bilateral agreement. i am all for environmental sustainability because the future does not belong to us. where i think we must be careful, however, is in recognising that the many elements which need to come into play to provide a satisfactory response to the climate change challenge – from emission caps to financing – cannot be translated into provisions in our trade agreements. i think there is a wider forum for that and, provided that there is an agreement in the wider forum, then of course such an agreement has to be reflected in the bilateral free trade agreements. whether it is also possible in the development round that we have just discussed, the doha round, is much more questionable because there is certainly not agreement among all the participants in this multilateral process to have a climate chapter in the final outcome. however, our position will be that we are in favour of this. lastly, on mr désir’s report, i think this comes at a very timely moment, given that a new commission communication on corporate social responsibility (csr) is in preparation. the commission and the members of the oecd are actively contributing to updating the current oecd benchmarks in time for the oecd ministerial meeting in may 2011. in all our csr-related activities, we will carefully consider various options for promoting responsible behaviour by european companies, irrespective of their place of operation, and with special regard to feasibility and consequences. let me add that this is not only a matter of trade, or of bilateral and multilateral trade agreements. in the united states, legislation was recently adopted whereby multinational companies – and not only those with their operations in the united states but also those with their registered offices there – are required to be responsible and to produce certification of their financial operations and transactions with respect to raw materials. i think it is a very laudable initiative which is, in fact, completely outside bilateral agreements. most of these operations concerning raw materials are not covered by bilateral agreements, they are simply financial and industrial operations by multinational companies, but if they have their registered offices in the united states, then the united states can take action vis-à-vis such companies. i think it would be a very good idea for us to consider doing exactly the same with respect to european companies that are active mostly in third world countries, and then to extend the same approach to countries like canada and australia, so that we would ultimately encompass the majority of these kinds of industrial activities and extractive industries in the world. i think this would be a considerable contribution to development in sustainable conditions. in short, congratulations for the three reports. i am certainly willing to continue the discussion on these subjects with you in the coming months and years.

in writing. you are certainly aware of the difficulties facing the european union once again when it comes to voting on the 2011 budget. the european commission and the european parliament wanted an increase of around 5% to implement the new european policies (regulation of financial markets, common foreign policy, etc.) made necessary by the challenges we are facing. given the current budgetary constraints, the european parliament ultimately preferred to reduce this increase to 2.91% provided that certain political conditions were met (debate on the allocation of the european union's own resources to put an end to the negotiations between member states, flexibility on the budget, financing of the major strategic priorities). the council of the european union refusing these conditions, i supported this new resolution of the european parliament because it clearly reaffirms the position of the european parliament which is both reasonable, constructive and ambitious. while my colleagues and i wish to contribute to the effort being made across europe, we also wish to underline the importance of european contributions to the coordination and support of policies across the union.
in writing. i voted in favour of this resolution because it recalls, in technical terms, the three requirements which condition the parliament's vote on the 2011 budget, namely the maintenance of the flexibility instrument, a budgetary instrument necessary to ensure the minimum financing of community competences and priorities, the commitment of the european commission to make concrete proposals on new own resources by july 2011, and the strong involvement of parliament in future debates on the european union's financing system, specifically on the issue of own resources and the development of the next financial framework. this resolution reaffirms the changes brought about by the treaty of lisbon to the council so that it finally recognises the new legitimacy of parliament in budgetary matters. beyond the battle between institutions, we must be aware that it is the question of european integration and the future of the community project itself that is at stake in this debate on the budget, with parliament embodying the renewal of the community spirit and respect for the citizens of the union. finally, the member states which have ratified this treaty individually must take all the necessary measures and fulfil the stated ambitions.

in writing. the european union, thanks to the external competences granted to it by the european treaties, concludes numerous trade agreements every year. as the european union is expanding its competences in the field of human rights (inclusion of the charter of fundamental rights in primary law) and sustainable development (one of the five major europe 2020 objectives), i felt it was important to support the report by my colleague tokia saifi to better take these issues into account in the union's trade agreements. it naturally proposes to strengthen cooperation within existing international organisations, to systematise the inclusion of clauses on these matters, but also innovates by calling for the creation of a world environment organisation, which could be seized in the event of environmental dumping. the scheme also contains the possibility of a carbon inclusion mechanism. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the proposal. this dual instrument would thus make it possible to combat emissions transfers to third countries.
in writing. international trade agreements should be an opportunity for the eu to promote social and environmental standards with its partners. the report, adopted by a large majority, contains proposals to ensure that imported products comply with the same social and environmental standards as european products and that in the event of social or environmental dumping, there should be a possibility of appeal both to the ilo and to a world environmental organisation which should be set up rapidly. the free trade agreements currently under negotiation must contain clauses on human rights but also on economic, social and environmental standards to be respected; what 's the matter ? the eu will no longer be able to cope with unfair competition from low-cost but lower-quality imports. the future of european agriculture is at stake, but also that of the european industrial sector.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report on human rights and social and environmental standards in international trade agreements because it is essential that eu trade policy is consistent with its political objectives. the text, substantially improved by the s&d group, makes it clear that trade can no longer be an end in itself but that any agreement must now respect a number of social and environmental clauses. these clauses will have to be binding and there are possibilities for referral, in particular to the un high commissioner for human rights.
in writing. the report highlights a number of relevant issues such as the periodic review of the application of the human rights clause in trade agreements by the un human rights council, the possibility of referral to the office of the united nations high commissioner for human rights by the ilo, the involvement of national parliaments and third country citizens in negotiations and the fight against modern slavery. this concern for human rights is appreciated by a parliament which has endorsed the coup d'état in honduras and the signing of a trade agreement with the putschists. but beyond my doubts as to the real significance of the human rights text, the desire to establish free trade agreements everywhere and the promotion of the exchange of polluting rights, the so-called 'carbon market', prevent me from voting for this text.
in writing. in 2009, the european ombudsman received 3098 complaints, of which 727 were within his mandate. established by the maastricht treaty in 1992, this intermediary between european citizens and the union's authorities is empowered to receive complaints from european citizens and businesses, but also from institutions or any person legally resident or domiciled in a member state. elected by the european parliament at the beginning of its parliamentary term and for its entire term, he investigates any cases of maladministration brought to his attention. it shall draw up an annual report on its activities. by voting for this resolution, i am adding my voice to the general approval of the european parliament for the action of this essential link in democracy.
in writing. the european audiovisual tradition has allowed the emergence of a pluralistic media model based on a dual system. this original system provides a place for public service operators and commercial operators who balance each other in a complementary relationship. the digital revolution places new constraints on this dual system. the arrival of new communication channels, alternative networks, is putting the old order at risk. to preserve the complementarity of the old system and make room for new channels of communication, european broadcasting needs to be reformed. this is the meaning of the resolution i voted for, which attempts to meet the triple challenge of modernisation, convergence and respect for pluralism.
in writing. the eu regularly calls for freedom of expression to be respected in many third countries, but it must itself be virtuous and respect this principle. the resolution, adopted by a large majority on 25 november, calls on the member states to put an end to political interference in the content of public broadcasters and recalls that respect for european standards on freedom of expression, media pluralism and independence, and the funding of public service media should be a priority for all member states. parliament called on the commission to take the necessary steps to ensure that the rules on the free movement of goods are respected and to ensure that the rules on the free movement of goods are applied in all member states. parliament also took the opportunity of this vote to recall that media independence requires appropriate and stable funding for public service media and transparency of the ownership of private broadcasters. finally, the member states are asked to adopt their legislation on public service broadcasting on the internet, adapting copyright to the new digital age.
in writing. it is rare in this house to see a public service advocate. i am not sure that a dual system necessarily allows for media pluralism, and i do not think that it is possible to free the private media from financial logic, but i welcome a text which advocates the maintenance of the public service broadcasting. it is the only one that can be controlled by the sovereign people and can allow everyone to have access to pluralistic and quality information, which is not the case in france today or in several countries dominated by the oligarchy.
in writing. broadcasting is at the heart of a technological revolution: the digitisation of media content and its accessibility via the internet has revolutionised the broadcasting paradigm. in the 1970s, commercial and private actors struggled to obtain broadcasting frequencies in the face of state monopolies. today, the proliferation of possibilities for consumers to access multimedia content requires us to define the necessary balance between public service and private media. what do we recommend in this report? the public service needs special attention, in the face of media concentration and commercial competition, to contribute, without political interference, to the maintenance of a public sphere providing high quality programmes and objective information. we ask the states to allocate sufficient resources to support the digitisation of the public service and, above all, to combat a dangerous digital divide. rural or urban environments, poor or disadvantaged populations, all must have equal and quality access to public service broadcasting. finally, given the income disparity between giants like google and those they refer, we need to think about how search engines can better contribute to funding content creation.

in writing. with just a few days to go before the opening of the cancún climate change conference, the joint resolution voted by parliament calls on 'the heads of state and government of the world to show real authority and political will during the negotiations'. concrete and rapid action is needed because the evidence is compelling: our commitments as they stand are not likely to minimise the damage of climate change. in short, our governments need to do more, and faster. the european union must play a leading role in the negotiations by speaking with one voice to weigh in against china and the united states. on targets, we call for more ambition: we need to adopt a target of 30% reduction of greenhouse gas emissions in the union by 2020 compared to 1990 levels (paragraph 16). it is true that the fight against climate change has become one of the major political challenges in recent years, but we have not yet had the desired results: energy efficiency and the 20% rate of renewable energies to be achieved by 2020, for example, are not on the agenda! cancun is an opportunity to do better, let's not miss it...again!
in writing. the european union will have to speak with one voice and be ambitious and persuasive at the climate change conference in cancún, lest the failure of copenhagen be repeated. concrete and rapid action is needed because the evidence is compelling: our commitments as they stand are not likely to minimise the damage of climate change. the european union must play a leading role in the negotiations by speaking with one voice to weigh in against china and the united states. the major objective to be achieved is a 30% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions in the union by 2020 compared to 1990 levels. we also need to get a commitment from industrialized countries like the united states to developing countries to help them fight and adapt to climate change, by fighting deforestation, desertification, etc. it is time for our governments to take stock of the climate challenges ahead and to build a political consensus to put in place a truly global policy to combat climate change.
in writing. the european union adopted an ambitious target in 2008 under the french presidency to reduce its co2 emissions by 20% by 2020. this objective is already very difficult to win over the other countries involved in the international climate change negotiations. in the absence of an international agreement, this european objective may also imply a loss of competitiveness at international level for european companies in certain sectors of the economy. proposing a new target of 30% reduction in co2 emissions in the european union is therefore completely disproportionate and that is why i voted against this draft resolution. the position adopted by parliament today does not put the european union in a credible negotiating position with its partners to reach an agreement at the cancún conference next month.
in writing. after the failure of the copenhagen conference and the many disappointed hopes for the setting of ambitious targets to combat climate change, the european union must commit itself with conviction to achieving a convincing result at the cancun conference. we have therefore adopted a resolution in the european parliament calling for the european union to increase its commitment to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions by 2020 from 20% to 30%. i voted in favour of this resolution because i believe that there is no time to lose and that if we wait and procrastinate, it will be too late. the european union must create momentum within the international community to achieve real results.
in writing. i voted against the final adoption of this resolution. the lack of realism in the objectives that have been voted is striking. the unilateral adoption by the eu of a 30% emission reduction target by 2020 would have a serious impact on competitiveness and employment in france. there are too many uncertainties in the negotiations for the eu to set such binding targets. last year europe made the mistake of thinking that it could impose its vision on its partners in copenhagen. if the eu makes these mistakes again, there is no way it will even be at the negotiating table. we can talk about 30% when an international agreement is reached on this figure.
in writing. i voted for the resolution on the cancun climate change conference because, following the failure of the last copenhagen conference, it is more urgent than ever that the european union should have strong objectives in a united way. the text reaffirms the objective of reducing greenhouse gas emissions in the union by 30% by 2020, with a view to limiting the global temperature rise to 2°c. the text, realistic, takes account of the 'common but differentiated' responsibility of states according to their level of development and growth. it also provides for the creation of a 'green fund' to meet the financing needs, with priority for vulnerable countries.
in writing. this resolution takes up many of the points made in the cochabamba contribution. i welcome this and am surprised that it is not mentioned anywhere in the text. it proposes to define and enforce the principle of climate justice and acknowledges without mentioning it the climate debt owed by the countries of the north to the countries of the south. the objectives it proposes for reducing greenhouse gas emissions are in line with those set by the ipcc. energy sobriety, although the word is not yet in use, is finally on the agenda. if the exchange of polluting rights known as the 'carbon market' and the establishment of a 'global carbon market' were not one of the main points of this text, i could have voted for it.
in writing. serious incidents have recently occurred again in western sahara. this territory, which was administered by spain until 1976, remains the subject of intense tensions between the moroccan authorities and the independence campaigners. the western sahara, which lies between the atlantic, mauritania and southern morocco, was divided between these two countries by the spanish. the resolution proposed by some of my colleagues on the tragedy of 24 october was drafted in a hurry, even though a certain degree of restraint is essential on such matters. i have therefore decided to abstain on this text and to follow the current investigation closely.
in writing. the violence in western sahara, in the gdim izik camp during its dismantling and in the town of laayoune, is serious and must be strongly condemned. the european parliament is right to express its concern at the deterioration of the situation in the region. as the un has recalled, the parties to the conflict must agree to reach a realistic, just, lasting and mutually acceptable political solution in accordance with the relevant un security council resolutions. however, i regret that this text was drawn up without waiting for parliament to have the tangible facts and precise data on the circumstances that led to this tragedy and on the exact number of victims. journalists, independent investigators, observers and political leaders must be allowed access to the city of laayoune and the refugee camps in order to be able to shed light on these events in a calm manner. the plight of the sahrawi people must not be used to encourage further violence.
in writing. like my colleagues, i deplore the recent events in western sahara and wish to express my solidarity with all the families of the victims. however, i refused to join this resolution which contains many factual errors, omits key facts and does not objectively report on the violence that erupted on 8 november 2010. the resolution should have been guided by prudence and by tangible and indisputable evidence. instead, this unbalanced text makes a hasty and uninformed judgment on the situation and discredits, without any foundation, the independent investigation carried out by the moroccan authorities. i regret this partisan statement made in haste because it weighs on the climate of informal negotiations at the un between the kingdom of morocco and the polisario front and has generated tensions on the ground. we are losing sight of what should be our priority: the search for a balanced and mutually acceptable agreement between the two sides to restore stability and security to the civilian population. we must absolutely avoid opening a new front in the sensitive sahel region and preserve our strategic partnership with morocco.
in writing. since the collapse of the ussr, ukraine has become a major issue in european geopolitics. it has regained its independence, but is still an integral part of the 'near abroad' defined by moscow. in order to fully enjoy its freedom of action and to highlight its strong historical links with the european union, ukraine has for some time been making known its intention to join the member states of the european union. ukraine, rich in natural resources and located in the heart of a key region, should be seen as a strategic pivot for the european union. i voted in favour of the european parliament resolution which welcomes ukraine's european orientation. it is, however, a reminder of the progress that this fragile democracy still has to make. at the same time, it notes the important efforts and significant progress that the country has made in recent times. if it is measured, it affirms ukraine's european destiny.
in writing. in december 2009, the un climate summit took place, where unfortunately the european union was not able to play the role it wanted. as a leader in sustainable development, it is important that it extends this commitment to international trade policies. that is why, at the opening of the cancún summit, my colleagues in the european parliament and i wanted to give a voluntary mandate to the delegation which will defend the european positions. we call on the european commission to discriminate between imported products on the basis of their ecological footprint and to establish a carbon footprint of all trade policies. recalling that the fight against climate change is a factor of competitiveness, our resolution calls for the awareness of all industrial sectors to the problem of carbon leakage and the end of fossil fuel subsidies, in particular tax exemptions for air transport.
in writing. the report by yannick jadot points out that trade in goods and services is responsible for around 20% of global greenhouse gas emissions and that this should be taken into account in the fight against climate change. while the european union has put in place ambitious climate policies, it is essential that trade policies also reflect this political imperative. i join the rapporteur in deploring the fact that some countries, by subsidizing energy prices and applying no co2 restrictions or quotas, could benefit from a comparative advantage. it is regrettable that these countries have no interest in joining multilateral agreements on climate change and are encouraging unfair competition in this respect. the european union's trade policy is not an end in itself but must remain a political instrument for regulation. we must ensure fair competition and refuse to allow our climate efforts to penalise us in global trade.
in writing. eu trade policies have an impact on the climate and the eu's responsibility cannot be limited to the greenhouse gas emissions it produces on its own territory. the european parliament adopted by a large majority this report which seeks to improve the coherence between trade and climate, making proposals on the discrimination of products according to their climate impact, and on the achievement of carbon accounting for all trade policies. while it is regrettable that some of the ambitious proposals have not been supported by the conservatives, the adoption of this report is still a clear call for a green transformation of our economy.
in writing. corporate social responsibility in international agreements promotes better governance of the global economy, promotes a fairer, more social and more humane globalisation and serves sustainable development. in the age of globalisation, i support this proposal to moralize international trade practices.
in writing. since the end of the second world war, the european union has benefited greatly from the opening up of international markets. on the other hand, we can regret that the european social model, which accompanied globalisation on the continent, has had little resonance in international trade negotiations. that is the subject of the resolution on which i voted this week. with this text i wished the union to take a strong position on the question of social dumping. it also called for the notion of corporate social responsibility, recognised by the oecd, the ilo and the united nations, to be integrated into the generalised system of preferences; the commission should carry out further impact studies to assess the effects of trade agreements on european smes; the commission has also proposed that these agreements now systematically include a clause on corporate social responsibility. as in the field of sustainable development, the european union must assert its convictions in the social model and make it a platform for progress in globalisation.
in writing. foreign investment is a very important economic issue for emerging and developing countries. however, given the weakness of social and environmental legislation in these countries, there are fears of abuses in terms of working conditions, human rights violations or environmental damage. this is why the european parliament has called for the inclusion of a social responsibility clause for companies investing in developing countries in trade agreements signed by the european union. this clause will make it possible to require clear and verifiable commitments from these companies, their subsidiaries and their supply chain regarding the social and environmental impact of their activity. it will also create a right of appeal for victims. this is a good response to raise the level of social and environmental protection requirements worldwide.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report on corporate social responsibility in trade agreements. globalisation has brought intense competition between countries, leading to intolerable abuses by many multinationals in developing countries in terms of working conditions, human rights violations and environmental damage. parliament called for a clause on corporate social responsibility to be included in all trade agreements signed by the european union. this clause will require the regular publication of reports on the social and environmental impact of the activities of companies, their subsidiaries and their supply chains. the report calls for judicial cooperation between the eu and signatory states and trade agreements to ensure effective access to justice for victims of violations of social and environmental legislation by multinationals and their subsidiaries.
in writing. corporate social responsibility can be a blink of an eye and a way of limiting certain abuses and suggesting that others are acceptable. however, it can provide a conceptual and legal framework for state intervention in production and its social and ecological conditions. i therefore support this text.
in writing. competition regulation is a pillar of the great internal market project that the european union has been pursuing since its creation. far from favouring large groups, competition policy aims to protect small operators against practices that distort competition. agreements between firms, for example to promote research programmes, may conceal an agreement to eliminate a competitor. on the contrary, the dynamism of the european economy is partly due to this capacity for cooperation. the european commission is therefore pursuing a pragmatic policy. it regularly sets out categories of agreements which must escape the rigorousness of the competition rules because they are ultimately beneficial. when it came to renewing these regulations, the european commission did a lot of consultation work. the draft regulation takes account of the european parliament's views and is in line with its views on the subject. i therefore voted in favour of this text.

the rapporteur. - madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, as you know, the european union has been trying to establish legislative instruments for economic immigration for more than ten years now. the commission has preferred a sectoral approach to an initially global approach. this proposal for a directive highlights the need for a common policy on legal immigration, particularly economic immigration. we have so far legislated on illegal immigration, border control, visa policy. it was time to move forward together on economic immigration, as the european union faces challenges common to all its member states, which require common solutions at european level. these challenges are the demographic decline and ageing of the european population. the overall employment forecasts show that there will be considerable labour shortages in the coming years as a result of these two problems affecting europe as a whole. so solutions need to be found at european level to meet the needs of the labour market and economic immigration is one of the solutions we need to explore. but be careful not to be mistaken. determining a european approach to the management of legal immigration means organising it, taking into account, of course, the needs and reception capacities of each member state. as stated in articles 1 and 8 of this proposal for a directive, the member states retain control over the number of migrants they wish to admit to their national territory. our governments have worked in various ways to regulate economic immigration - bilateral agreements, quotas, regulatory measures - but none of these measures have proved to be truly effective in managing legal migration flows and at the same time fighting illegal immigration. the link between the two is obvious. it is by organising legal immigration in an optimal way that we will succeed in putting an end to illegal immigration. and that is the whole point of the adoption of this package of measures presented by the commission five years ago. what will this 'single permit' directive bring to the existing legal landscape of economic immigration? unlike the blue card directive, this directive does not deal with the conditions of admission of workers from third countries, but it aims to eliminate the differences between the various national laws concerning the procedure for applying for a work permit and a residence permit, and the rights conferred on foreigners legally working in the european union. there is as yet no european instrument covering all the rights afforded to third-country nationals legally working and residing in the union. this directive will therefore put an end to these differences in protection between these workers by ensuring equal treatment with national workers in a significant number of areas: working conditions, education and vocational training, social protection, access to goods and services, tax benefits. this common framework thus aims to offer these people protection against exploitation by guaranteeing them the benefit of a secure and protective legal status. it also helps to combat unfair competition to the detriment of european workers. this differential in protection ultimately leads to the recruitment of low-skilled and weakly protected workers at the expense of european workers. the directive will also simplify the procedures for admission for employment purposes. all member states will have a standardised procedure which is simpler, cheaper and faster. the adoption of this directive will therefore bring major benefits to migrants, employers and national administrations and will ultimately allow for better management of legal migration flows. parliament is now a co-legislator, which means that it must also show responsibility - an idealistic and outdated view - we must be up to the new tasks that the lisbon treaty has given us. let us present ourselves as credible partners ready to take on the great challenge of managing the migratory pressure at europe's doorstep. we know that well-managed migration flows will be beneficial to all.
for the gue/ngl group madam president, commissioner, as mr cercas has very well pointed out, there is a disagreement between the committees on employment and freedom. our parliament should therefore refuse to vote on this so-called single licence directive. the text has, in fact, only one objective, if one reads it correctly, namely to put workers from the european union in competition with those from countries outside europe, and even immigrant workers with each other according to their status. if the directive remains as it is, there will be several statutes: that of residents, that of seasonal workers, that of workers transferred within the same undertaking. this would make it official that there are several categories of workers in the european union. accepting this would be a violation of the principles of the charter of fundamental rights. contrary to what you have said, madam rapporteur, with such differences in status, there is a permanent downward pressure on the living, working and employment conditions of all employees in the european union. equality cannot be reduced to the mere mention of working conditions. as mr cercas said, equality must concern wages, working time, job security, health, leave, social protection, access to public services, training. without this common minimum, it will be the jungle of competition, stigma, exclusion, exploitation without limits. equality must be the concern of all workers, regardless of their origin. we must not accept the addition of new forms of competition between workers to those introduced by the sinister bolkestein. equality between workers must be the subject of a single positive directive reaffirming this principle. if not, then it is in the name of workers' europe, social europe, a humanist europe that we all together, beyond our opinions, in this parliament, reject this directive.
madam president, i must admit that it is extremely curious to start a directive which aims to guarantee a legal framework for effective access to rights for all workers by a long list of exclusions of categories of workers from this directive. this is taking the form of the construction of legal migration but also of a european labour market in the form of thousands of leaves where each category of workers would be allocated, depending on their value, a kind of portfolio of rights. we are therefore very far from a horizontal and universal approach to workers' rights. i think that the european leaders have not yet understood that more rights for workers means more economic efficiency and more social cohesion, more individual and collective benefits for migrants, of course, for host societies and for societies of origin. as a study by the london school of economics shows, the regularization of 600 000 irregular workers in britain, who will not have access to this single application procedure, would bring three billion pounds into the british coffers. i don't think we're up to the challenge at all.
member of the commission. − mr president, this has indeed been a very good debate. regarding the scope of the directive, it is no secret that the commission would have liked a global approach. my predecessors proposed this many years ago. it was impossible. it still is, so we therefore have this sectoral approach. i do not like it, but it is the only way to move forward. the directive is necessary because we have third-country workers. they are in our countries and make an important contribution to our economies. we need to protect them. having said that, contrary to some of the views conditions and wages. it does not create discrimination. once adopted, the directive will be a very important tool in the fight for the protection of migrant workers and against social dumping. nobody wants social dumping. we want to protect these people. other categories of workers, such as seasonal workers and icts (intra-corporate transferees), are not included in the present proposal. i share
